$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}0 & -6 \\ 6 & 0\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{\alpha }_{0} & -6{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=6\text{i}t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=-6\text{i}t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r((6\text{i})t) & ={e}^{(6\text{i})t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}(6\text{i})t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}+6\text{i}{\alpha }_{1}t & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t &=\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ {\alpha }_{1} &=\frac{1}{6t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t & =6\cdot \frac{1}{6t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\cdot t \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186365668 :question/id #uuid "162963ac-9899-549d-9b3f-b09605170db6" :question/math-academy-id "q-334389"} {:db/id 17592186365673 :question/id #uuid The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 1 \\ 0 & -4\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & {\alpha }_{1}t \\ 0 & -4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The only eigenvalue of $At$ is 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-4t
$$

of multiplicity two. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(-4t) &={e}^{-4t} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda }r(-4t) &={e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}-4t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{-4t} \\ {\alpha }_{1} &={e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-4t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first one, we get

$$
-4t{e}^{-4t}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-4t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-4t}(1+4t).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}-4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =-4{e}^{-4t}t+{e}^{-4t}(1+4t) \\  & ={e}^{-4t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}t & ={e}^{-4t}t \\  & =t{e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-4t} & t{e}^{-4t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-4t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186442558 :question/id #uuid "9ce1dad2-2fca-5e8c-94e6-f02fef65fbf6" :question/math-academy-id "q-334378"} {:db/id 17592186442559 :question/id #uuid $$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus,

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 7\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 0 \\ 0 & 7{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=4t\,\text{and}\,{\lambda }_{2}=7t
$$

each of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(4t) &={e}^{4t} \\ r(7t) &={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}4t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{4t} \\ 7t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtract the first equation from the second one, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}=\frac{{e}^{7t}-{e}^{4t}}{3t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
4t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{4t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{7{e}^{4t}-4{e}^{7t}}{3}.
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the diagonal entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =4\cdot \frac{{e}^{7t}-{e}^{4t}}{3t}\cdot t+\frac{7{e}^{4t}-4{e}^{7t}}{3} \\  & ={e}^{4t} \\ 7{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =7\cdot \frac{{e}^{7t}-{e}^{4t}}{3t}\cdot t+\frac{7{e}^{4t}-4{e}^{7t}}{3} \\  & ={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{4t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{7t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048231} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3b918900-9d47-501a-8fe9-03921f6ed92d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "properties :topic/math-academy-id 6376} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186222332 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222502 :tutorial/content "Consider the homogeneous linear system

$$
\mathbf{x}' = A\mathbf{x},
$$

where $A$ is an $n\times n$ matrix.

A **fundamental matrix** for this system is an $n\times n$ matrix $\Phi(t)$ whose columns are $n$ linearly independent solutions of the system.

If $\mathbf{x}_1(t),\dots,\mathbf{x}_n(t)$ are linearly independent solutions, then one fundamental matrix is

$$
\Phi(t)=\big[\mathbf{x}_1(t),\dots,\mathbf{x}_n(t)\big].
$$

**Note:** The columns of $\Phi(t)$ can be written in any order.

Let's see an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "a7207a24-194d-59d6-b25c-f9bb4f1b0d6e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14508 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "3b0bd285-b383-5ebb-821f-4f74a0b37719" :step/math-academy-id 594316 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222333}} {:db/id 17592186222333 :step/content {:db/id 17592186221420 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186221191 :question/id #uuid "4874a486-2cf1-5b6e-ae4f-52579f03b077" :question/math-academy-id "e-21695"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "af871f3d-da9e-5fd3-a61f-94e155ccf2b3" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049851}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186221985} {:db/id 17592186221999} {:db/id 17592186308599} {:db/id 17592186308600} {:db/id 17592186308601} {:db/id 17592186398781} {:db/id 17592186442556} {:db/id 17592186442557} {:db/id 17592186442562}] :knowledge-point/title "Constructing a Fundamental Matrix"} :step/id #uuid "aa3c7790-3ab9-5519-bad3-4f82fc8ac113" :step/math-academy-id 594317 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222334}} {:db/id 17592186222334 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222503 :tutorial/content "Again, let $\Phi(t)$ be a fundamental matrix for the linear system

$$
\mathbf{x}' = A\mathbf{x},
$$

where $A$ is an $n\times n$ matrix. The fundamental matrices have the following important properties.

1\. *Satisfies the underlying system*. Indeed, since each column of $\Phi(t)$ is a solution of the system, we have

  $$
  \Phi'(t) = A\,\Phi(t).
  $$

2\. *Invertibility*. The columns of $\Phi(t)$ are linearly independent for all $t,$ so

  $$
  \det\Phi(t)\neq 0
  $$

  for all $t.$ In particular, $\Phi(t)$ is invertible for all $t.$

3\. *Representation of solutions*. Every solution $\mathbf{x}(t)$ of the system can be written in the form

  $$
  \mathbf{x}(t)=\Phi(t)\,\mathbf{c},
  $$

  where $\mathbf{c}$ is a constant vector.

4\. *Non-uniqueness*. If $C$ is any invertible constant matrix, then

  $$
  \Psi(t)=\Phi(t)\,C
  $$

  is also a fundamental matrix for the same system.

We'll now get some practice." :tutorial/id #uuid "e2fdbc29-4542-5fdc-adbd-316c5dcb6878" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14509 :tutorial/title "Properties of the Fundamental Matrix"} :step/id #uuid "2fe7252e-7fc7-59bb-bc32-74c452b7cf73" :step/math-academy-id 594320 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222335}} {:db/id 17592186222335 :step/content {:db/id 17592186221421 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186221193 :question/id #uuid "a52a6539-60d1-557c-a042-cbce5616e94f" :question/math-academy-id "e-21697"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "0aea7503-74d6-5ba4-9411-ee53e59512d0" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186221990} {:db/id 17592186221991} {:db/id 17592186311648} {:db/id 17592186311687} {:db/id 17592186365731} {:db/id 17592186391264} {:db/id 17592186396895} {:db/id 17592186396916} {:db/id 17592186442561} {:db/id 17592186498522} {:db/id 17592186498584}] :knowledge-point/title "Proving Properties of a Fundamental Matrix"} :step/id #uuid "2b90cd12-9695-5b6b-b407-6eed6ae7fc84" :step/math-academy-id 594321 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222336}} {:db/id 17592186222336 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222504 :tutorial/content "For a linear system $\mathbf{x}' = A\mathbf{x}$ with constant $n\times n$ matrix $A,$ the **standard fundamental matrix** is the unique fundamental matrix $\Phi_0(t)$ that satisfies the initial condition

$$
\Phi_0(0)=I_n,
$$

where $I_n$ is the $n \times n$ identity matrix.

For constant matrices $A,$ the standard fundamental matrix is given by

$$
\Phi_0(t)=e^{At}.
$$

This matrix satisfies

$$
\Phi_0'(t)=A\,\Phi_0(t)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\Phi_0(0)=I_n.
$$

**Note:** Any other fundamental matrix $\Phi(t)$ for the same system can be written in the form

$$
\Phi(t)=\Phi_0(t)\,C,
$$

where $C$ is an invertible constant matrix.

In the next slide, we will compute the standard fundamental matrix for a specific example." :tutorial/id #uuid "4f75576c-be32-5784-9fee-e1288445728c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14510 :tutorial/title "Fundamental Matrices and Matrix Exponentials"} :step/id #uuid "d44c84d5-4215-5318-bba2-81eb3a34ee7d" :step/math-academy-id 594325 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222337}} {:db/id 17592186222337 :step/content {:db/id 17592186221422 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186221192 :question/id #uuid "3e053d6d-f051-5c4c-a20b-1e90b2d5941b" :question/math-academy-id "e-21696"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "66c99cda-25a5-50f2-903b-bfb1fdc5fa10" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050054}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186221988} {:db/id 17592186221989} {:db/id 17592186308497} {:db/id 17592186308609} {:db/id 17592186308611} {:db/id 17592186308634} {:db/id 17592186365659} {:db/id 17592186365668} {:db/id 17592186365673} {:db/id 17592186442558} {:db/id 17592186442559} {:db/id 17592186442560} {:db/id 17592186498520}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing Fundamental Matrices Using Matrix Exponentials"} :step/id #uuid "32e0e465-9256-5f88-b771-2edff24ecd54" :step/math-academy-id 594326}] :activity/title "Fundamental Matrices" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186221468} {:db/id 17592186222332 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222502 :tutorial/content "Consider the homogeneous linear system

$$
\Phi(t)=\Phi_0(t)\,C,
$$

A=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 7\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the system of linear ODEs ${x}^{′}=Ax$ with the matrix $A$ shown above. Compute the **standard** fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ for this system.

<table align="l" cellpadding="0" rules="all">
<tbody><tr>
<td align="center" height="30px" rowspan="2">${Φ}_{0}(t)=\,\,$</td>
<td align="center" height="40px" width="5px"></td>
<td align="center" width="40px">{{field-1}}</td>
<td align="center" width="40px">{{field-2}}</td>
<td align="center" width="5px"></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td align="center"></td>
<td align="center">{{field-3}}</td>
<td align="center" width="30px">{{field-4}}</td>
<td align="center"></td>
</tr>
</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus,

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 7\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 0 \\ 0 & 7{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=4t\,\text{and}\,{\lambda }_{2}=7t
$$

each of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(4t) &={e}^{4t} \\ r(7t) &={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}4t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{4t} \\ 7t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtract the first equation from the second one, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}=\frac{{e}^{7t}-{e}^{4t}}{3t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
4t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{4t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{7{e}^{4t}-4{e}^{7t}}{3}.
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the diagonal entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =4\cdot \frac{{e}^{7t}-{e}^{4t}}{3t}\cdot t+\frac{7{e}^{4t}-4{e}^{7t}}{3} \\  & ={e}^{4t} \\ 7{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =7\cdot \frac{{e}^{7t}-{e}^{4t}}{3t}\cdot t+\frac{7{e}^{4t}-4{e}^{7t}}{3} \\  & ={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{4t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{7t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "3ad30acf-66b9-5977-ad36-2183bb8c58c8" :step/next {:db/id 17592186498619}} {:db/id 17592186498623 :step/content {:db/id 17592186365659 :question/answer-fields </tr></tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}0 & -6 \\ 6 & 0\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{\alpha }_{0} & -6{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=6\text{i}t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=-6\text{i}t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r((6\text{i})t) & ={e}^{(6\text{i})t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}(6\text{i})t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}+6\text{i}{\alpha }_{1}t & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t &=\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ {\alpha }_{1} &=\frac{1}{6t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t & =6\cdot \frac{1}{6t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\cdot t \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "3ea51f6a-6ea8-5162-ad6a-900689393007" :step/next {:db/id 17592186498620}} {:db/id 17592186498653 :step/content {:db/id 17592186498584 :question/answer-fields A derivation showing that every solution $x(t)$ can be written in the form $x(t)=Φ(t)\,c$ for some constant vector $c=[{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}]^{T}$ is given below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ be the columns of $Φ(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of solutions

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(t)$ can be written as $x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ $Φ(t)\,c={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $x(t)=Φ(t)\,c$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from line $\text{L2}$ by {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by the {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L5}$ follows from lines {{field-3}} by the transitive property of equality." :question/worked-solution "Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Once ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis, every solution $x(t)$ of the system can be expressed uniquely as a linear combination

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{the definition of a basis}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Since ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are the columns of $Φ(t),$ we can write

$$
Φ(t)=\begin{bmatrix}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}(t) & {x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Then by the definition of matrix multiplication,

$$
Φ(t)\,c=\begin{bmatrix}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}(t) & {x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{bmatrix}={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Thus, $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{definition of matrix multiplication}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}.$ In $\text{L3}$ we have $x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t),$ and in $\text{L4}$ we have $Φ(t)c={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).$ Since both expressions are equal to the same quantity, the transitive property of equality gives $x(t)=Φ(t)c.$ Thus, $\text{L5}$ follows from $\text{L3 and L4}.$"} :step/id #uuid :question/math-academy-id "q-336108" :question/problem "Consider the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant $2\times 2$ matrix. Let $Φ(t)$ be a fundamental matrix for this system. A derivation showing that every solution $x(t)$ can be written in the form $x(t)=Φ(t)\,c$ for some constant vector $c=[{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}]^{T}$ is given below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ be the columns of $Φ(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of solutions

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(t)$ can be written as $x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ $Φ(t)\,c={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $x(t)=Φ(t)\,c$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from line $\text{L2}$ by {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by the {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L5}$ follows from lines {{field-3}} by the transitive property of equality." :question/worked-solution "Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Once ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis, every solution $x(t)$ of the system can be expressed uniquely as a linear combination

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{the definition of a basis}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Since ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are the columns of $Φ(t),$ we can write

$$
Φ(t)=\begin{bmatrix}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}(t) & {x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Then by the definition of matrix multiplication,

$$
Φ(t)\,c=\begin{bmatrix}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}(t) & {x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{bmatrix}={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Thus, $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{definition of matrix multiplication}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}.$ In $\text{L3}$ we have $x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t),$ and in $\text{L4}$ we have $Φ(t)c={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).$ Since both expressions are equal to the same quantity, the transitive property of equality gives $x(t)=Φ(t)c.$ Thus, $\text{L5}$ follows from $\text{L3 and L4}.$"} :step/id #uuid A=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 7\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the system of linear ODEs ${x}^{′}=Ax$ with the matrix $A$ shown above. Compute the **standard** fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ for this system.

<td align="center" height="30px" rowspan="2">${Φ}_{0}(t)=\,\,$</td>

<td align="center" width="40px">{{field-1}}</td>

</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus,

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 7\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 0 \\ 0 & 7{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=4t\,\text{and}\,{\lambda }_{2}=7t
$$

each of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(4t) &={e}^{4t} \\ r(7t) &={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}4t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{4t} \\ 7t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtract the first equation from the second one, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}=\frac{{e}^{7t}-{e}^{4t}}{3t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
4t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{4t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{7{e}^{4t}-4{e}^{7t}}{3}.
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the diagonal entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =4\cdot \frac{{e}^{7t}-{e}^{4t}}{3t}\cdot t+\frac{7{e}^{4t}-4{e}^{7t}}{3} \\  & ={e}^{4t} \\ 7{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =7\cdot \frac{{e}^{7t}-{e}^{4t}}{3t}\cdot t+\frac{7{e}^{4t}-4{e}^{7t}}{3} \\  & ={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{4t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{7t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "3ad30acf-66b9-5977-ad36-2183bb8c58c8" :step/next {:db/id 17592186498619}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "dae93f70-eae4-559e-a461-fdfe0abd280a" :answer/type {:db/id :topic/math-academy-id 344} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186065206 :step/content {:db/id 17592186065396 :tutorial/content "When a function $y=y(x)$ contains complex products, quotients, or radicals, we can use logarithmic differentiation to find the derivative $y'(x).$ 

For example, consider the following function: 

$$
y = x^2 \cdot 2^x
$$

 

Our goal is to find $y'(x).$ To do this, we will use the product rule for logarithms, namely

$$
\ln(a b)= \ln a + \ln b.
$$

 

We differentiate our function by following four steps.

**Step 1.** We take the natural logarithm of both sides and apply the product and power rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}\cdot {2}^{x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})+\operatorname{ln}⁡({2}^{x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡x+x\operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2.** Next, we differentiate both sides of our equation using implicit differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2\operatorname{ln}⁡x+x\operatorname{ln}⁡2) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =2\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{′}+(x)^{′}\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(2) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =2\cdot \frac{1}{x}+1\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(2) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{2}{x}+\operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3.** Then, we solve for $y'{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(\frac{2}{x}+\operatorname{ln}⁡2)\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4.** Finally, we substitute back our original expression for $y =x^2\cdot 2^x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & ={x}^{2}\cdot {2}^{x}(\frac{2}{x}+\operatorname{ln}⁡2) \\  & =x\cdot {2}^{x+1}+{x}^{2}\cdot {2}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1895a7f3-5ba4-5a31-85b3-6a7b050b307c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6088 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "caef414d-4f2a-5504-9b92-39a03d2f3c8f" :step/math-academy-id :step/content {:db/id 17592186065397 :tutorial/content "In cases where we wish to differentiate a quotient of functions

$$
y =  f(x) = \dfrac{g(x)}{h(x)},
$$

we can apply the quotient rule for logarithms: 

$$
\ln \left(\dfrac{a}{b}\right) = \ln a - \ln b
$$

 

For example, let's compute $y',$ where the function $y$ is given by

$$
y = \dfrac {e^{x^2}}{(1-2x)^2(x-1)^3}.
$$

First, we find the natural logarithm of both sides and use the quotient and power rules for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{(1-2x)^{2}(x-1)^{3}}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{{x}^{2}})-\operatorname{ln}⁡((1-2x)^{2})-\operatorname{ln}⁡((x-1)^{3}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & ={x}^{2}-2\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-2x)-3\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-1)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}-2\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-2x)-3\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-1)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =2x-2\cdot \frac{1}{1-2x}\cdot (-2)-3\cdot \frac{1}{x-1} \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =2x+\frac{4}{1-2x}-\frac{3}{x-1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for $y'{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(2x+\frac{4}{1-2x}-\frac{3}{x-1})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute our expression for $y,$ and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{(1-2x)^{2}(x-1)^{3}}(2x+\frac{4}{1-2x}-\frac{3}{x-1}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{(1-2x)^{2}(x-1)^{3}}(\frac{2x(1-2x)(x-1)+4(x-1)-3(1-2x)}{(1-2x)(x-1)}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{(1-2x)^{3}(x-1)^{4}}(2x(1-2x)(x-1)+4(x-1)-3(1-2x)) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{(1-2x)^{3}(x-1)^{4}}(-4{x}^{3}+6{x}^{2}+8x-7) \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{(1-2x)^{3}(x-1)^{4}}(4{x}^{3}-6{x}^{2}-8x+7) \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}(4{x}^{3}-6{x}^{2}-8x+7)}{(1-2x)^{3}(x-1)^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "8cf6e625-669a-5fda-b756-e1ce091eaa93" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6090 :tutorial/title "Using Logarithms to Differentiate a Quotient"} :step/id #uuid "2141558f-a6d2-515d-902a-620581d72401" :step/math-academy-id 37041 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065208}}] :activity/title "Further Logarithmic Differentiation" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186064435} {:db/id 17592186065206 :step/content {:db/id 17592186065396 :tutorial/content "When a function $y=y(x)$ contains complex products, quotients, or radicals, we can use logarithmic differentiation to find the derivative $y'(x).$

**Step 2.** Next, we differentiate both sides of our equation using implicit differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2\operatorname{ln}⁡x+x\operatorname{ln}⁡2) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =2\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{′}+(x)^{′}\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(2) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =2\cdot \frac{1}{x}+1\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(2) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{2}{x}+\operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3.** Then, we solve for $y'{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(\frac{2}{x}+\operatorname{ln}⁡2)\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4.** Finally, we substitute back our original expression for $y =x^2\cdot 2^x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & ={x}^{2}\cdot {2}^{x}(\frac{2}{x}+\operatorname{ln}⁡2) \\  & =x\cdot {2}^{x+1}+{x}^{2}\cdot {2}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1895a7f3-5ba4-5a31-85b3-6a7b050b307c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6088 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "caef414d-4f2a-5504-9b92-39a03d2f3c8f" :step/math-academy-id 37035 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065207}} {:db/id 17592186065396 :tutorial/content "When a function $y=y(x)$ contains complex products, quotients, or radicals, we can use logarithmic differentiation to find the derivative $y'(x).$ 

For example, consider the following function: 

$$
y = x^2 \cdot 2^x
$$

 

Our goal is to find $y'(x).$ To do this, we will use the product rule for logarithms, namely

$$
\ln(a b)= \ln a + \ln b.
$$

 

We differentiate our function by following four steps.

**Step 1.** We take the natural logarithm of both sides and apply the product and power rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}\cdot {2}^{x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})+\operatorname{ln}⁡({2}^{x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡x+x\operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2.** Next, we differentiate both sides of our equation using implicit differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2\operatorname{ln}⁡x+x\operatorname{ln}⁡2) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =2\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{′}+(x)^{′}\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(2) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =2\cdot \frac{1}{x}+1\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(2) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{2}{x}+\operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3.** Then, we solve for $y'{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(\frac{2}{x}+\operatorname{ln}⁡2)\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4.** Finally, we substitute back our original expression for $y =x^2\cdot 2^x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & ={x}^{2}\cdot {2}^{x}(\frac{2}{x}+\operatorname{ln}⁡2) \\  & =x\cdot {2}^{x+1}+{x}^{2}\cdot {2}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1895a7f3-5ba4-5a31-85b3-6a7b050b307c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6088 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186065207 :step/content {:db/id 17592186064309 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186064146 :question/id #uuid "c24da7ef-0070-5aae-bade-c82ea56476ba" :question/math-academy-id "e-9845"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "7613eee3-a281-57cb-bc47-3b1594920bd1" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048773} {:db/id 17592186050375}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186064655} {:db/id 17592186064662} {:db/id 17592186506517} {:db/id 17592186506521} {:db/id 17592186506543} {:db/id 17592186506546} {:db/id 17592186506581}] :knowledge-point/title "Differentiating a Product"} :step/id #uuid "b6a516b4-d0c4-5ec7-8f7e-12edd0e85c51" :step/math-academy-id 37036 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065210}} {:db/id 17592186065210 :step/content {:db/id 17592186065397 :tutorial/content "In cases where we wish to differentiate a quotient of functions

$$
y =  f(x) = \dfrac{g(x)}{h(x)},
$$

we can apply the quotient rule for logarithms: 

$$
\ln \left(\dfrac{a}{b}\right) = \ln a - \ln b
$$

 

For example, let's compute $y',$ where the function $y$ is given by

$$
y = \dfrac {e^{x^2}}{(1-2x)^2(x-1)^3}.
$$

First, we find the natural logarithm of both sides and use the quotient and power rules for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{(1-2x)^{2}(x-1)^{3}}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{{x}^{2}})-\operatorname{ln}⁡((1-2x)^{2})-\operatorname{ln}⁡((x-1)^{3}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & ={x}^{2}-2\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-2x)-3\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-1)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}-2\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-2x)-3\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-1)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =2x-2\cdot \frac{1}{1-2x}\cdot (-2)-3\cdot \frac{1}{x-1} \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =2x+\frac{4}{1-2x}-\frac{3}{x-1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for $y'{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(2x+\frac{4}{1-2x}-\frac{3}{x-1})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute our expression for $y,$ and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{(1-2x)^{2}(x-1)^{3}}(2x+\frac{4}{1-2x}-\frac{3}{x-1}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{(1-2x)^{2}(x-1)^{3}}(\frac{2x(1-2x)(x-1)+4(x-1)-3(1-2x)}{(1-2x)(x-1)}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{(1-2x)^{3}(x-1)^{4}}(2x(1-2x)(x-1)+4(x-1)-3(1-2x)) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{(1-2x)^{3}(x-1)^{4}}(-4{x}^{3}+6{x}^{2}+8x-7) \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}}{(1-2x)^{3}(x-1)^{4}}(4{x}^{3}-6{x}^{2}-8x+7) \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{{x}^{2}}(4{x}^{3}-6{x}^{2}-8x+7)}{(1-2x)^{3}(x-1)^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "8cf6e625-669a-5fda-b756-e1ce091eaa93" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6090 :tutorial/title "Using Logarithms to Differentiate a Quotient"} :step/id #uuid "2141558f-a6d2-515d-902a-620581d72401" :step/math-academy-id 37041 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065208}} {:db/id 17592186065208 :step/content {:db/id 17592186064310 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186064147 :question/id #uuid "7db11c8c-344b-5d87-a8ae-3b006e5bd92b" :question/math-academy-id "e-9846"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "71dd9228-4b05-54d9-aeb2-3bdabf89e0e9" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049079} {:db/id 17592186050542}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186064653} {:db/id 17592186064663} {:db/id 17592186506513} {:db/id 17592186506532} {:db/id 17592186506564} {:db/id 17592186506577} {:db/id 17592186506591}] :knowledge-point/title "Differentiating a Quotient"} :step/id #uuid "57a60273-bc58-5aff-8dcd-d7139782aa2a" :step/math-academy-id 37037 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065209}} {:db/id 17592186065209 :step/content {:db/id 17592186064311 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186064148 :question/id #uuid "e0cec84d-96cf-5fed-ba05-a5cfc57841a1" :question/math-academy-id "e-9847"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "c6005f9a-3eba-5f8d-909d-894d9cd24d12" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050208} {:db/id 17592186050496} {:db/id 17592186050887} {:db/id 17592186050894}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186064652} {:db/id 17592186064654} {:db/id 17592186233441} {:db/id 17592186506509} {:db/id 17592186506518} {:db/id 17592186506527} {:db/id 17592186506552} {:db/id 17592186506582}] :knowledge-point/title "Differentiating a Radical Expression"} :step/id #uuid "8850f22e-33ee-545a-8f5e-4dc37bda3b30" :step/math-academy-id 37038} {:db/id 17592186065397 :tutorial/content "In cases where we wish to differentiate a quotient of functions

Sketch the phase portrait of the linear system above." :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we have
![](images/73/737c96109e65d59f4df2c2fa574737fe604483fe4ccc9772a3d2bf22ee32e55a.svg)
where ![](images/22/22dbda7d3b169206071e5af49fd1fe1af28d86ef1e0a8b37d58eacb62b44c1d2.svg)

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvalues are $\lambda_1=\lambda_2=-8$ with the corresponding eigenvectors $\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ and ![](images/5b/5bd691bbaa9542184d90e55aeb16f4dfcd3d22d092b4652e8bddba7bf0b926aa.svg)

The general solution of the system is
![](images/8b/8b25789fb45234e4299e4b5ce3371c1afafc181c64f9802d212ae7cbefc0970f.svg)

Notice that for each vector ![](images/67/674212f0d815e0588faaf276bd797e9822ac5659e5d4b15a7635d7f1327d5dc5.svg) we get the straight-line solutions of the form
![](images/d4/d4c31285e6f31a229bc6fc5cbe2d78e2bf50f73bb6305d91687c5dcc31c3885a.svg)
that represent the line passing through the origin and parallel to the vector ![](images/26/268764bbe776b03647daac7fc77e8ed24107e1bb0cf16d955f7a845a12c65755.svg)

$$

where $w$ is a solution to the equation $(A-\lambda I)w=v.$

In our case, 

$$
\lambda =-1,\,v=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix},\,w=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 
Thus, the general solution of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix} & ={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-t}+{c}_{2}(\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}t{e}^{-t}+\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-t}) \\  & ={c}_{1}{e}^{-t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{c}_{2}{e}^{-t}\begin{bmatrix}t \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{-t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$
lie on the $x\text{-axis}.$ Since ${e}^{-t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach $\text{the origin}$ as $t\to \infty .$

:topic/math-academy-id 3240} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186167860 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168023 :tutorial/content "In this topic, we'll study phase portraits of linear systems
![](images/6f/6f6a92e2b8fb89f833268a5526876cb3af5215db0193a2aaaad8aac5790752ea.svg)
where the $2 \times 2$ matrix $A$ has a *repeated* real eigenvalue $\lambda$ (algebraic multiplicity $2$).

If $A$ has *two independent eigenvectors*, then $A$ is the scalar matrix
![](images/69/69199c6f84ebe1f9587b9207a3f1fc42c909fc9a1e43041e11fcab9ce881e5d1.svg)
In this case, every direction through the origin behaves like an eigenvector direction, and trajectories are straight lines:

$$
\mathbf{x}(t)=e^{\lambda t} \mathbf{v}, \qquad \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^2.
$$

So the phase portrait is a **star node**:

- If $\lambda>0,$ trajectories move *away* from the origin and we have an **unstable star node**.

- If $\lambda<0,$ trajectories move *toward* the origin and we have a **stable star node**.

Let's see an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "8fe5f0d1-38d4-5cd2-98f8-8935d82677de" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14569 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "b7f1536f-3909-5575-8eee-90d0181e7613" :step/math-academy-id 588332 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167861}} {:db/id 17592186167861 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168005 :tutorial/content "Let's sketch the phase portrait of the following linear system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &=2x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t) &=2y(t)\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Writing our system in matrix form, we have
![](images/f5/f58fb57caaba8c5f6a110c72565c24803ac233f41b8eb2db0c5221bcf12d7fe2.svg)
where ![](images/65/65298928a44147868c82da753a731e35c3aa0ad5e4b3400819d9d9f16f546a34.svg)

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvalues are $\lambda_1=\lambda_2=2$ with the corresponding eigenvectors $\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ and ![](images/69/694a89326f61bbbba7e91db5dcb607a74f99881ce16059450dbe1bbac7ee797e.svg)

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}.$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=-2$ with the corresponding eigenvectors $\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ and $\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.$

The general solution of the system is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{-2t}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{c}_{2}{e}^{-2t}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}={e}^{-2t}\begin{bmatrix}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Notice that for each vector $\begin{bmatrix}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{bmatrix},$ we get the straight-line solutions of the form
${e}^{-2t}\begin{bmatrix}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{bmatrix}$
that represents the line passing through the origin and parallel to the vector $\begin{bmatrix}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{bmatrix}.$

Since ${e}^{-2t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$

"4f56e312-a8c4-5c65-9893-3ebc38120b4d" :knowledge-point/title "Distinguishing Between Max/Min and Argmax/Argmin"}] :question/problem "Let $S=\{-1,0,2,4\}$ and suppose
$f(-1)=3,\qquad f(0)=-2,\qquad f(2)=5,\qquad f(4)=1$.
Compute the following:
$\max_{x \in S} f(x),\qquad \arg\max_{x \in S} f(x),\qquad \min_{x \in S} f(x),\qquad \arg\min_{x \in S} f(x)$." :question/worked-solution "Recall that

- $\max\limits_{x \in S} f(x)$ is the largest output value, while
- $\arg\max\limits_{x \in S} f(x)$ is an input in $S$ where that largest output occurs.

On the other hand,

- $\min\limits_{x \in S} f(x)$ is the smallest output value, while
- $\arg\min\limits_{x \in S} f(x)$ is an input in $S$ where that smallest output occurs.

The outputs of $f$ on $S$ are
$3,\qquad -2,\qquad 5,\qquad 1$.
The largest output is $5$, and it occurs at $x=2$. Therefore,

$$
\max_{x \in S} f(x)=5, \qquad \arg\max_{x \in S} f(x)=2
$$

Similarly, the smallest output is $-2$, and it occurs at $x=0$. Therefore,

$$
\min_{x \in S} f(x)=-2, \qquad \arg\min_{x \in S} f(x)=0
$$"} {:db/id 17592186049707} {:db/id 17592186049900} {:db/id 17592186231733 :question/id #uuid "6aa9e0d5-9851-5891-b86f-1e8060798b8c" :question/math-academy-id "q-355205"} {:db/id 17592186231742 :question/id #uuid "6f68d534-8f10-5941-a10d-ac65abf5c7b1" :question/math-academy-id "q-355267" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186231450 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "4f56e312-a8c4-5c65-9893-3ebc38120b4d" :knowledge-point/title "Distinguishing Between Max/Min and Argmax/Argmin"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/id #uuid "cbe9032c-6f44-58dc-9ddc-fa3ca07c4b0d" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186231036} {:answer-field/id #uuid "e873c666-a858-5034-8acf-044865f6f906" :answer-field/key "field-4" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186231037} {:answer-field/id #uuid "1ee2f779-c391-500f-97a7-e605497c97aa" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186231038} {:answer-field/id #uuid "6d82f40d-9e66-5857-827e-a182d65aadbe" :answer-field/key "field-3" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186231039}] :question/problem "Let $S = {2, 4, 6, 8}$ and suppose

Consider the expression
$x^*=\arg\max_{x \in S} f(x)$.
What does this statement mean in words? Also, what does $\max_{x \in S} f(x)$ represent?" :question/worked-solution "The expression

$$
x^*=\arg\max_{x \in S} f(x)
$$

means that:

- $x^*$ is an input value in $S$.
- Among all $x \in S$, the value $f(x^*)$ is as large as possible.

In other words, $x^*$ is a choice of input where $f$ attains its largest value on $S$.

By contrast, $\max_{x \in S} f(x)$ is not an input. It is the largest *function value* that $f$ attains on $S$."} {:db/id 17592186231736 :question/id #uuid "fc34c1a3-91bd-5e9d-9f78-3fda5d46cb89" :question/math-academy-id "q-355208"} {:db/id :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186231870 :step/content {:db/id 17592186232041 :tutorial/content "In a previous lesson, we used $\max$ and $\min$ to talk about the largest and smallest *values* a function can take on a set.

In this lesson, we learn two closely related pieces of notation:

- $\max$ and $\min$ return the best (largest/smallest) *function value*.
- $\arg\max$ and $\arg\min$ return the *input value* (the "argument") where that best value occurs.

For example, let

$$
S = \{1,2,3\}
$$

and suppose

$$
f(1)=4,\qquad f(2)=7,\qquad f(3)=6
$$

Then the largest function value is $7$, and it occurs when $x=2{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
max_(x ∈ S)f(x) &= 7, \\
\arg max_(x ∈ S)f(x) &= 2
\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, $\min_{x \in S} f(x)$ is the smallest function value, and $\arg\min_{x \in S} f(x)$ is an input where that smallest value occurs.

**Watch out!** Sometimes the best value occurs at more than one input. In that case, we need to clarify what $\arg\max$ (or $\arg\min$) means. We will handle this after we practice the basic case." :tutorial/id #uuid "bba3a61c-b816-520d-909b-990b65f4c370" :tutorial/math-academy-id 15114 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "f81d5a0b-4aa5-57a2-8cd4-4289eca1c411" :step/math-academy-id 629516 :step/next {:db/id 17592186231871}} {:db/id 17592186231871 :step/content {:db/id 17592186231450 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186231376 :question/id #uuid "6308dcce-94b4-57ff-9d03-a184ad2048bb" :question/math-academy-id "e-22126"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "4f56e312-a8c4-5c65-9893-3ebc38120b4d" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049707} {:db/id 17592186049900}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186231733} {:db/id 17592186231742}] :knowledge-point/title "Distinguishing Between Max/Min and Argmax/Argmin"} :step/id #uuid "2c4bb6ef-8180-592f-a235-299caf0aa949" :step/math-academy-id 629517 :step/next {:db/id 17592186231872}} {:db/id 17592186231872 :step/content {:db/id 17592186232042 :tutorial/content "Sometimes a function attains its largest (or smallest) value at more than one input. In that case, there are multiple inputs that satisfy the definition of $\arg\max$ (or $\arg\min$).

In this course, when a tie occurs, we report the *set* of all inputs where the maximum is achieved as follows:

$$
\arg\max_{x \in S} f(x) = {x \in S{:} f(x) = \max_{u \in S} f(u)}
$$

Similarly, when a tie occurs, we report the set of all inputs where the minimum is achieved as follows:

$$
\arg\min_{x \in S} f(x) = {x \in S{:} f(x) = \min_{u \in S} f(u)}
$$

The quantities $\max_{x \in S} f(x)$ and $\min_{x \in S} f(x)$ are still single numbers." :tutorial/id #uuid "8ef1fb19-42d3-5471-a53f-023f932c2ad2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 15115 :tutorial/title "Argmax and Argmin With Ties"} :step/id #uuid "4d293468-053f-5f98-87b1-78b1633c6e5a" :step/math-academy-id 629520 :step/next {:db/id 17592186231873}} {:db/id 17592186231873 :step/content {:db/id 17592186231451 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186231377 :question/id #uuid "b8e4dcaf-38c1-5244-9bca-2e0eab32c34c" :question/math-academy-id "e-22127"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "258ff70f-5f41-5ea6-a0c2-bf74e7ce1cff" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186231734} {:db/id 17592186231735}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing Argmax and Argmin With Ties"} :step/id #uuid "316698db-832d-542a-826d-ce5cc6c0afb4" :step/math-academy-id 629521 :step/next {:db/id 17592186231874}} {:db/id 17592186231874 :step/content {:db/id 17592186231452 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186231378 :question/id #uuid "c901e488-7c50-5af5-85b2-ce70b1447a8c" :question/math-academy-id "e-22128"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "24771a14-af10-5bc8-94d4-17c28b180c84" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186231736} {:db/id 17592186231737}] :knowledge-point/title "Writing and Reading Formal Notation"} :step/id #uuid "8ba7e4ab-2bfb-5d57-8de9-e8f4b6255634" :step/math-academy-id 629524}] :activity/title "Argmax and Argmin Notation" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186231551} {:db/id 17592186231870 :step/content {:db/id 17592186232041 :tutorial/content "In a previous lesson, we used $\max$ and $\min$ to talk about the largest and smallest *values* a function can take on a set.

:knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186096731 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f354f758-3745-5cee-9a4b-a0878c2c8578" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Area Bounded by a Parametric Curve"}] :question/problem "![](images/e9/e933e484b931ee54b345a8e7af3b0e44f80a8b019e3e401007ad4987192e33be.png)

Find the area bounded between the curve defined parametrically as
$x = t^2 - 1, \qquad y = t^3 - 4t$
and the $x$-axis for $t \in [-2,0]$." :question/worked-solution "The unsigned area bounded by the parametric curve

$$
x = x(t), \qquad y = y(t), \qquad t_1 \leq t \leq t_2
$$

and the $x$-axis is given by the absolute value of the integral

$$
\int_{t_1}^{t_2} y \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} \:\textrm{d}t
$$

First, we compute

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{dx}{dt} &= \frac{d}{dt}(t^{2} - 1) \\
&= 2t
\end{aligned}
$$

So, we obtain the integral expression

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}y\frac{dx}{dt}dt &= \int_{-2}^{0}(t^{3} - 4t)(2t)dt \\
&= 2\int_{-2}^{0}t^{2}(t^{2} - 4)dt
\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that this integral will give us a negative number since

$$
y\dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} \leq 0
$$

for all $t \in [-2,0]$.

Therefore, the area is

$$
\begin{aligned}
A &= -2\int_{-2}^{0}t^{2}(t^{2} - 4)dt \\
&= 2\int_{-2}^{0}t^{2}(4 - t^{2})dt \\
&= 2\int_{-2}^{0}(4t^{2} - t^{4})dt \\
&= 8\int_{-2}^{0}t^{2}dt - 2\int_{-2}^{0}t^{4}dt \\
&= 8 \cdot \left.\frac{t^{3}}{3}\right|_{-2}^{0} - 2 \cdot \left.\frac{t^{5}}{5}\right|_{-2}^{0} \\
&= 8(\frac{0^{3}}{3} - ((-2)^{3})/(3)) - 2(\frac{0^{5}}{5} - ((-2)^{5})/(5)) \\
&= 8(\frac{8}{3}) - 2(\frac{32}{5}) \\
&= \frac{64}{3} - \frac{64}{5} \\
&= \frac{128}{15}
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186050929} {:db/id 17592186096926 :question/id #uuid "ca12c5dd-889a-50f3-8378-1f36935574a5" :question/math-academy-id "q-10215"} {:db/id 17592186097235 :question/id #uuid "8f616c95-e646-5708-bd6d-cb015c8c8c27" :question/math-academy-id "q-37370"} {:db/id 17592186527964 :question/id #uuid "8222fa21-5fa3-52f1-a894-4b100aeb534d" :question/math-academy-id "q-10207"} {:db/id 17592186096758 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186096561 :question/id #uuid "95cdc31d-c3f2-50b6-9447-b7317af775f9" :question/math-academy-id "e-7412"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f20da72e-5a93-5a4e-be39-d412bd8fee86" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048946} {:db/id 17592186050531}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186097133 :question/id #uuid "ad65213f-7896-5eb3-8900-a92c0319ea40" :question/math-academy-id "q-15688"} {:db/id 17592186097134 :question/id #uuid "21fbf351-adf3-5745-8c52-bdb88804c75c" :question/math-academy-id "q-15696"}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding an Integral Expression for the Area Bounded by a Parametric Curve"} {:db/id 17592186096561 :question/id #uuid "95cdc31d-c3f2-50b6-9447-b7317af775f9" :question/math-academy-id "e-7412" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186096758 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f20da72e-5a93-5a4e-be39-d412bd8fee86" :knowledge-point/title "Finding an Integral Expression for the Area Bounded by a Parametric Curve"}] :question/problem "![](images/3d/3dd84b2e84056a4e6c71f7b76534f5a6f1a46132ea5da5ed8edb2a514b9ea6b4.png)

Find an integral expression for the area bounded between the curve defined parametrically as
$x = e^{-t^2}, \qquad y = t^3$,
and the $x$-axis for $0 \leq t \leq \sqrt{2} \,$?" :question/worked-solution "The unsigned area bounded by the parametric curve

$$
x = x(t), \qquad y = y(t), \qquad t_1 \leq t \leq t_2
$$

and the $x$-axis is given by the absolute value of the integral

$$
\int_{t_1}^{t_2} y \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} \:\textrm{d}t
$$

First, we compute

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{dx}{dt} &= \frac{d}{dt}(e^{-t^{2}}) \\
&=-2te^{-t^{2}}
\end{aligned}
$$

So, we obtain the integral expression

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}y\frac{dx}{dt}dt &= \int_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}t^{3}(-2te^{-t^{2}})dt \\
&=-2\int_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}t^{4}e^{-t^{2}}dt
\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that this integral will give us a negative number since

$$
y\dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} \leq 0
$$

for all $t \in [0, \sqrt{2}]$.

Therefore, the area is given by

$$
A = -\left(-2 \int_{0}^{\sqrt{2}} t^4 e^{-t^2} \, \textrm{d}t \right) = 2 \int_{0}^{\sqrt{2}} t^4 e^{-t^2} \, \textrm{d}t

Consider the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x=t^3-1, \qquad y=2t-t^3, \qquad t \in (-\infty, \infty)
$$

The shaded area shown in the diagram is the finite region bounded between the curve, the $x$-axis, and the vertical lines formed by $x$-axis and the points on the curve corresponding to $t_1=0$ to $t_2=1$, as shown.

We know that the area of the curve is given by

$$
A = \int_{a}^{b} y \:\textrm{d}x
$$

Since our curve is defined parametrically, we need to change the variable of integration from $x$ to $t$ using the change of variables formula, given by

$$
A = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} y(t) \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm d t}\:\textrm d t
$$

Now, in this case, we have

$$
\frac{dx}{dt} = \frac{d}{dt}(t^{3} - 1) = 3t^{2}
$$

Applying the change of variables formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
A &= \int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}y(t)\frac{dx}{dt}dt \\
&= \int_{0}^{1}(2t - t^{3}) \cdot 3t^{2}dt \\
&= \int_{0}^{1}6t^{3} - 3t^{5}dt \\
&= 6\int_{0}^{1}t^{3}dt - 3\int_{0}^{1}t^{5}dt \\
&= 6 \cdot \left.\frac{t^{4}}{4}\right|_{0}^{1} - 3 \cdot \left.\frac{t^{6}}{6}\right|_{0}^{1} \\
&= 6(\frac{1}{4} - 0) - 3(\frac{1}{6} - 0) \\
&= \frac{3}{2} - \frac{1}{2} \\
&= 1
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the shaded area shown in the picture has an area of $1$ square unit." :tutorial/id #uuid "1d0c890f-fbe0-5ded-948b-b94d13caac3b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1083 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "786032d8-d66a-579e-8336-348ca609cfb8" :step/math-academy-id 2136 :step/next {:db/id 17592186097747}} {:db/id 17592186097613 :step/content {:db/id 17592186096731 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186096538 :question/id #uuid "85879186-0866-5159-905b-65d043681231" :question/math-academy-id "e-604"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f354f758-3745-5cee-9a4b-a0878c2c8578" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050929}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186096926} {:db/id 17592186097235} {:db/id 17592186527964}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Area Bounded by a Parametric Curve"} :step/id #uuid "296a64b2-a271-5186-bf37-e47d7b56624c" :step/math-academy-id 2138} {:db/id 17592186097653 :step/content {:db/id 17592186096758 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186096561 :question/id #uuid "95cdc31d-c3f2-50b6-9447-b7317af775f9" :question/math-academy-id "e-7412"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f20da72e-5a93-5a4e-be39-d412bd8fee86" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048946} {:db/id 17592186050531}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186097133} {:db/id 17592186097134}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding an Integral Expression for the Area Bounded by a Parametric Curve"} :step/id #uuid "3a032caf-6330-5e24-bafb-d45c348ad375" :step/math-academy-id 27495 :step/next {:db/id 17592186097613}} {:db/id 17592186097747 :step/content {:db/id 17592186097915 :tutorial/content "In general, the area between the $x$-axis and the parametric curve

$$
x = x(t), \qquad y = y(t), \qquad t_1 \leq t \leq t_2
$$

is given by the absolute value of the integral

$$
\int_{t_1}^{t_2} y \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} \:\textrm{d}t
$$

Note the following:

- When applying this formula, we assume that the chosen parametrization traverses the curve only once.
- It's possible that this integral gives a negative value for the area even when the corresponding region lies entirely above the $x$-axis! To see why, note that if the curve lies above the $x$-axis, we must have $y(t) > 0$. However, if the curve is parameterized so that it is traversed from right to left, then $\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t} < 0$, and we have
$y\cdot \dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t} < 0$
and thus, our integral turns out to be negative.
- To ensure that we get an unsigned area, we take the absolute value of the integral.
- In general, care must be taken when asked to compute the area bounded by a parametric curve when $y\dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}$ changes sign over the domain of integration. However, we won't consider that scenario here.

{:db/id 17592186499598 :step/content {:db/id 17592186499639 :tutorial/content "We can use what we know about rounding numbers to approximate ratios.
We round the quantities to a given degree first, before setting up the ratio.

Look at the following table, which shows the number of girls in a ballet school with blonde or black hair.

| Blonde Hair | Black Hair |
| --- | --- |
| $33$ | $58$ |

Rounding to the nearest ten, let's determine the approximate ratio of girls with blonde hair to girls with black hair.

First, let's approximate the number of girls with blonde or black hair by rounding to the nearest ten.

- Number of girls with blonde hair: $33 \longrightarrow 30$

- Number of girls with black hair: $58 \longrightarrow 60$

Therefore, the ratio of the number of girls with blonde hair to the number of girls with black hair is approximately

$$
\dfrac{30}{60}.
$$

We can simplify this ratio by dividing both numbers by $10$:

$$
\dfrac{30 \div 10}{60 \div 10} = \dfrac{3}{6}
$$

Then, we divide by $3$:

$$
\dfrac{3 \div 3}{6 \div 3} = \dfrac{1}{2}
$$

Therefore, the ratio of the number of girls with blonde hair to the number of girls with black hair is approximately $\dfrac{1}{2}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "777fe794-e3cc-5250-a9e8-e407cc3f306c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2052 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "805b138d-9de3-5c18-96bd-507752cfcb3d" :step/math-academy-id 648000 :step/next {:db/id 17592186499610}} {:db/id 17592186499607 :step/content {:db/id 17592186499634 :tutorial/content "Now, let's see how we can find a value given the ratio and another value.

Suppose at a school library, there are some science books and $396$ history books. The ratio of the number of science books to the number of history books is $3: 4.$ By rounding the number of history books to the nearest ten, approximate the number of science books in the library.

First, let's approximate the number of history books:

$$
396 \longrightarrow 400
$$

The ratio of the number of science books to the number of history books is

$$
\dfrac{\color{blue}3}{\color{red}4}.
$$

  

Here, 

- the numerator represents the number of science books, and

- the denominator represents the number of history books.

We can make a denominator of $400$ by multiplying the numerator and denominator by $100{:}$

$$
\dfrac{3 \times 100}{4 \times 100} = \dfrac{300}{400}
$$

Therefore, there are approximately $300$ science books in the library." :tutorial/id #uuid "16e103a1-de00-5acb-9566-24168dec17eb" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14923 :tutorial/title "Finding a Value Given a Ratio"} :step/id #uuid "9d54fdb2-7a7b-5fda-81dd-61e03fb3fa56" :step/math-academy-id 648008 :step/next {:db/id 17592186499581}} {:db/id 17592186499610 :step/content {:db/id 17592186499435 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186499520 :question/id #uuid "a8368c62-f936-54c5-b069-1adabcb11ffe" :question/math-academy-id "e-2281"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "10523576-ab54-5731-bfaf-999a591295e0" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186499446} {:db/id 17592186499456} {:db/id 17592186499477} {:db/id 17592186499530} {:db/id 17592186499559}] :knowledge-point/title "Approximating Ratios by Rounding to the Nearest Ten"} :step/id #uuid "aa6626df-e1ca-57ff-8e3c-685699ee9c0c" :step/math-academy-id 648001 :step/next {:db/id 17592186499591}}] :activity/title "Approximating Ratios" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186498720} {:db/id 17592186499598 :step/content {:db/id 17592186499639 :tutorial/content "We can use what we know about rounding numbers to approximate ratios.

Suppose at a school library, there are some science books and $396$ history books. The ratio of the number of science books to the number of history books is $3: 4.$ By rounding the number of history books to the nearest ten, approximate the number of science books in the library.

First, let's approximate the number of history books:

$$
396 \longrightarrow 400
$$

The ratio of the number of science books to the number of history books is

$$
\dfrac{\color{blue}3}{\color{red}4}.
$$

  

Here, 

- the numerator represents the number of science books, and

- the denominator represents the number of history books.

We can make a denominator of $400$ by multiplying the numerator and denominator by $100{:}$

$$
\dfrac{3 \times 100}{4 \times 100} = \dfrac{300}{400}
$$

Therefore, there are approximately $300$ science books in the library." :tutorial/id #uuid "16e103a1-de00-5acb-9566-24168dec17eb" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14923 :tutorial/title "Finding a Value Given a Ratio"} {:db/id 17592186049227 :topic/difficulty 0.7978510291583273 :topic/encompasses [{:db/id 17592186429443 :encompassing/rationale "Initial Codex estimate from captured target-band crossing frequency. 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "$\int \frac{4{x}^{2}}{(2x+1)^{3}}\,\text{d}x=$" :question/worked-solution "First, we must convert the integrand into a sum of partial fractions:

$$
\frac{4{x}^{2}}{(2x+1)^{3}}=\frac{A}{2x+1}+\frac{B}{(2x+1)^{2}}+\frac{C}{(2x+1)^{3}}
$$

To determine the coefficients $A,B,$ and $C,$ we first multiply both sides of the above equation by $(2x+1)^{3}$ and get

$$
4{x}^{2}=A(2x+1)^{2}+B(2x+1)+C.
$$

Plugging in $x=-\frac{1}{2},$ we can eliminate $A$ and $B$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}4{(-\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =A{(2\cdot (-\frac{1}{2})+1)}^{2}+B(2\cdot (-\frac{1}{2})+1)+C \\ 1 & =C\end{aligned}
$$

Now, plugging in $x=0$ and substituting the known value of $C,$ we get an equation relating $A$ and $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}4(0)^{2} & =A(2(0)+1)^{2}+B(2(0)+1)+C \\ 0 & =A+B+1 \\ A+B & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, plugging in $x=-1$ and substituting the known value of $C,$ we get an equation relating $A$ and $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}4(-1)^{2} & =A(2(-1)+1)^{2}+B(2(-1)+1)+C \\ 4 & =A-B+1 \\ A-B & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the equations $A-B=3$ and $A+B=-1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2A & =3-1 \\ A & =1,\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting back into $A+B=-1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}1+B & =-1 \\ B & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integrand as the partial sum:

$$
\frac{4{x}^{2}}{(2x+1)^{3}}=\frac{1}{2x+1}-\frac{2}{(2x+1)^{2}}+\frac{1}{(2x+1)^{3}}.
$$

Finally, we integrate this expression term by term to get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{4{x}^{2}}{(2x+1)^{3}}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{1}{2x+1}-\frac{2}{(2x+1)^{2}}+\frac{1}{(2x+1)^{3}})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{2x+1}\,\text{d}x-2\int \frac{1}{(2x+1)^{2}}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{1}{(2x+1)^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x+1|+\frac{1}{2x+1}-\frac{1}{4(2x+1)^{2}}+K,\end{aligned}

:step/content {:db/id 17592186070036 :tutorial/content "Suppose we are given the integral  $\displaystyle \int \dfrac{3x+2}{(x+1)^2} \textrm{d}x.$ Note that we have the repeated factor $(x+1)$ in the denominator. 

The correct form of the partial fraction expansion of the integrand is
 

$$
\dfrac{3x+2}{(x+1)^2}=\dfrac{A}{(x+1)} +\dfrac{B}{(x+1)^2} \,.
$$

To determine the coefficients $A$ and $B,$ we first multiply both sides the above equation by $(x+1)^2$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}3x+2 & =A(x+1)+B.\end{aligned}
$$

Plugging in $x=-1,$ we can eliminate $A$ and solve for $B\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}3(-1)+2 & =A(-1+1)+B \\ B & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Plugging in $x=0$ and substituting the known value of $B,$ we can solve for $A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}3(0)+2 & =A(0+1)+B \\ 2 & =A+B \\ 2 & =A-1 \\ A & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\dfrac{3x+2}{(x+1)^2}= \dfrac{3}{(x+1)} -\dfrac{1}{(x+1)^2}.
$$

Now this function can be integrated term by term. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3x+2}{(x+1)^{2}}\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{3}{(x+1)}-\frac{1}{(x+1)^{2}})\text{d}x \\  & =3\int \frac{1}{x+1}\text{d}x-\int \frac{1}{(x+1)^{2}}\text{d}x \\  & =3\operatorname{ln}|x+1|+\frac{1}{x+1}+C\,,\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/title "Reading Argmax and Argmin From a Table"}] :question/problem "| $x$ | $f(x)$ |
| --- | ---: |
| $-2$ | $3$ |
| $-1$ | $0$ |
| $0$ | $5$ |
| $1$ | $-1$ |
| $2$ | $2$ |

The table above gives values of $f$ on the set $S=\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}$. Use the table to compute
$\max_{x \in S} f(x),\qquad \arg\max_{x \in S} f(x),\qquad \min_{x \in S} f(x),\qquad \arg\min_{x \in S} f(x)$." :question/worked-solution "Recall that

- $\max\limits_{x \in S} f(x)$ is the maximum output value, while
- $\arg\max\limits_{x \in S} f(x)$ is an input in $S$ where that maximum output occurs.

On the other hand,

- $\min\limits_{x \in S} f(x)$ is the minimum output value, while
- $\arg\min\limits_{x \in S} f(x)$ is an input in $S$ where that minimum output occurs.

The output values in the table are $3,0,5,-1$, and $2$.

The largest output is $5$, and it occurs at $x=0$. Therefore,

$$
\max_{x \in S} f(x)=5 \qquad \textrm{and} \qquad \arg\max_{x \in S} f(x)=0
$$

The smallest output is $-1$, and it occurs at $x=1$. Therefore,

$$
\min_{x \in S} f(x)=-1 \qquad \textrm{and} \qquad \arg\min_{x \in S} f(x)=1
$$"} {:db/id 17592186231738 :question/id #uuid "e70e47da-52c7-50e8-856b-58fb79d6db30" :question/math-academy-id "q-355210"} {:db/id 17592186231740 :question/id #uuid "dd1993cf-74ad-51ff-8a2d-45ff7871e237" :question/math-academy-id "q-355222" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186231453 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "c20e9719-4699-5c80-92a1-714717021bb1" :knowledge-point/title "Reading Argmax and Argmin From a Table"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/id #uuid "939237bf-2795-5991-9195-c9aac7c4a8ec" :answer-field/key "field-4" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186231028} {:answer-field/id #uuid "a032fd09-81da-5080-bac6-e08f1ba44250" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186231029} {:answer-field/id #uuid "f42e362e-2b11-5082-86a7-df66b5608efb" :answer-field/key "field-3" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186231030} {:answer-field/id #uuid "5a9e6834-bc16-5837-a2a7-9a04b63440de" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186231031}] :question/problem "| $t$ | $h(t)$ |

"113b981d-bbf2-588a-be74-028506cdb19d" :knowledge-point/title "Sketching the Phase Portrait of a System"}] :question/problem "Consider the system of linear differential equations below.

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &=-y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t) &=9x(t)\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The eigenvalues of the system's matrix are $\lambda_{1,2} = \pm3\text{i},$ for which the corresponding eigenvectors are $\mathbf{v}_{1,2} = [\pm \text{i}, 3]^T,$ respectively. Given that the general solution of the system is
![](images/2b/2bc77eafe7c4362a1020c1f547a19ef0e72c309ebb82d1480e2ffec5bdfd8b38.svg)
sketch the phase portrait of the system of differential equations given above." :question/worked-solution "We are given that the general solution of the system is
![](images/b0/b0df9855fa710d30217ffbe12135de27a9aa50e55b639418829b649ee6eb420c.svg)

For example, when $c_1=1$ and $c_2=0,$ we obtain the following curve:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=-\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ y &=3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Computing the coordinates (rounded to two decimal places) of several points on the curve, we get the table below.

| $t$ | $0$ | $\dfrac{\pi}{12}$ | $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $x$ | $0$ | $-0.71$ | $-1$ |
| $y$ | $3$ | $2.12$ | $0$ |

Let's sketch this solution in the phase space.

![](images/3c/3c2ea4467854f749e07f5ae3922273a2ebd441da4fb9df834ce0676157e856a2.png)

Notice that $|\sin(3t)| \leq 1$ and $|\cos(3t)| \leq 1.$ Thus, the obtained curve is bounded. So, we have an ellipse that is traversed counterclockwise.

The phase portrait of our system looks as follows:

![](images/6d/6d13d0dfadac45d40b74cb7e740a880305098f0939e2f45d74706c4022183c54.png)" :question/worked-solution "Let $\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{p}+\mathbf{q}\text{i},$ where $\mathbf{p},\mathbf{q} \in \mathbb{R}^2,$ be an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda = a + b\text{i}.$

Then, a complex solution of the system is given by

$$
\mathbf{x}_{\text{complex}}(t) = \mathbf{v} e^{\lambda t}.
$$

Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{complex}}(t) & =v{e}^{(a+b\text{i})t} \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt))(p+q\text{i}) \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+\text{i}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\textbf{x}(t) = 
c_1 e^{at}\big(\cos(bt)\mathbf{p}-\sin(bt)\mathbf{q}\big) + 
c_2 e^{at}\big(\sin(bt)\mathbf{p}+\cos(bt)\mathbf{q}\big),
$$

where the parts $\big(\cos(bt)\mathbf{p}-\sin(bt)\mathbf{q}\big)$ and $\big(\sin(bt)\mathbf{p}+\cos(bt)\mathbf{q}\big)$ are bounded.

Now notice that the given curve is unbounded, representing a spiral that is traversed counterclockwise. Thus, we must have $a \neq 0.$

Also, notice that the spiral is traversed toward the origin.

Hence, to insure that $e^{at} \to 0,$ we require $a < 0.$"} {:db/id 17592186048535} {:db/id 17592186167229 :question/id #uuid "0d2fdbc8-ed30-59a9-869b-569e3f094dfe" :question/math-academy-id Then, a complex solution of the system is given by

$$
{x}_{\text{complex}}(t)=v{e}^{\lambda t}.
$$

Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{complex}}(t) & =v{e}^{(a+b\text{i})t} \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt))(p+q\text{i}) \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+\text{i}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\text{x}(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+{c}_{2}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q),
$$

where the parts $(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)$ and $(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q)$ are bounded.

Now, notice that the given curve is $\text{bounded}$ (and closed), representing $\text{an ellipse}$ that is traversed $\text{counterclockwise}.$

But we have that:

- ${e}^{at}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty $ when $a>0,$ and

- ${e}^{at}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty $ when $a<0.$

Then, a complex solution of the system is given by

$$
\mathbf{x}_{\text{complex}}(t) = \mathbf{v} e^{\lambda t}.
$$

Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{complex}}(t) & =v{e}^{(a+b\text{i})t} \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt))(p+q\text{i}) \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+\text{i}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\textbf{x}(t) = 
c_1 e^{at}\big(\cos(bt)\mathbf{p}-\sin(bt)\mathbf{q}\big) + 
c_2 e^{at}\big(\sin(bt)\mathbf{p}+\cos(bt)\mathbf{q}\big),
$$

where the parts $\big(\cos(bt)\mathbf{p}-\sin(bt)\mathbf{q}\big)$ and $\big(\sin(bt)\mathbf{p}+\cos(bt)\mathbf{q}\big)$ are bounded.

Now, notice that $a = \text{Re}(\lambda) = 0$ and $e^{at} = e^{0\cdot t} = 1$ for all $t.$ Thus, we have an ellipse that curves around the origin.

the equilibrium point (origin) is {{field-2}}." :question/worked-solution "Let $v=p+q\text{i},$ where $p,q\in {R}^{2},$ be an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =a+b\text{i}.$

Then, a complex solution of the system is given by

$$
{x}_{\text{complex}}(t)=v{e}^{\lambda t}.
$$

Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{complex}}(t) & =v{e}^{(a+b\text{i})t} \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt))(p+q\text{i}) \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+\text{i}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\text{x}(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+{c}_{2}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q),
$$

where the parts $(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)$ and $(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q)$ are bounded.

Now, notice that $a=\text{Re}(\lambda )=5>0$ and ${e}^{at}={e}^{5t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty .$ Thus, we have a spiral that is traversed toward infinity as $t\to \infty .$ 

Therefore, since $\text{Re}(\lambda )>0,$ the equilibrium point (origin) is $\text{an unstable spiral (source)}.$"} {:db/id 17592186050780} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid :topic/math-academy-id 3241} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186167904 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168009 :tutorial/content "In this topic, we'll study phase portraits of linear systems
![](images/b0/b083c5707c4e9aed3141fe638c55a1ed2dc3ad6569f122bef307550c94fe6a8b.svg)
where the eigenvalues of a ![](images/25/2521651122403a440e682fef383af333958f5b0d1334abe8b0771865d4daf100.svg) matrix ![](images/32/3207697e43e4f88223ad85c16964c3103a50c0c999a4ca14417695158d45526b.svg) are
![](images/ee/eee119e3e35f381a1d66d9e1e75b27d89e68d5f72307f4e792887d5d7e9d0099.svg)

Let ![](images/37/37030865839993f96fced21145844e8fca9c6d44e7922c623fe8e0bef98ef154.svg) where ![](images/0d/0d26960845a9f13b07c87e80faa88162c1dda64123f13567958d00aaa0a4dc94.svg) be an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue ![](images/fa/faa0f885195eacb91222dc9ccc18cf7ab891a17bd787359d13bf4e72bf09d703.svg)

Then, a complex solution of the system is given by
![](images/c4/c44ac9f2de14beffd3411373047316c888a93815d2f90d338f500ca329f66355.svg)

Using Euler's formula, we obtain
![](images/e9/e90f20affdff00fd5fb24e5b6f75c31d42a0e5b2ad52b38b2d4456ee6555bfc8.svg)

Therefore, the general solution of the system is
![](images/62/6224eb38da8f189696cbda057a5568d71310d64574d36e80af6e1a11ceed6d6e.svg)

Notice that ![](images/42/42bbe4d12055825e9c24b2dfc1a6ca306cb2675c13d039fbdb67e2170788c612.svg) and ![](images/ca/ca0400387ee619b6e2ddc7028859cf5902aecb715c38ec71e43b0f9056533cb6.svg) are bounded, so the factor ![](images/b0/b051bd1eb312485960edb54d28ffe85da63acab1c5f20b59466d01f55cba034c.svg) controls the long-term behavior:

- If ![](images/0a/0a23a6577131711d405eb650b1d9d8429ca07d07bb9759644c407121643dcf5e.svg) then ![](images/9a/9a15a0d668c2a7ab9457f6a4c605858e03ddbb3ff93f3667d0deb0def1e206b1.svg) as ![](images/e5/e54727d514ed264e6dd30c7f4044746e6d2b4b462dc3776daecf7eb68634c358.svg) So, trajectories are *unbounded*, and we have a *spiral* that is traversed toward infinity as ![](images/e5/e54727d514ed264e6dd30c7f4044746e6d2b4b462dc3776daecf7eb68634c358.svg) In particular, the trajectory is unbounded for ![](images/bb/bb0d93faa0ccc44575fe83f9f7a644895ced86c18e9908a8e0d6dc6a36378d7d.svg)

- If ![](images/28/28e6012b2b10c0a7f40681ab8a73666a12afd6e976c59f536ed30d1defca5f64.svg) then ![](images/2b/2b74153553b7dab9ad3a92e31ddd3b09ba44e4ba0e451229e924f227087fb58b.svg) as ![](images/e5/e54727d514ed264e6dd30c7f4044746e6d2b4b462dc3776daecf7eb68634c358.svg) So, trajectories *approach the origin*, and we have a *spiral* that is traversed toward the origin as ![](images/e5/e54727d514ed264e6dd30c7f4044746e6d2b4b462dc3776daecf7eb68634c358.svg) In particular, the trajectory is bounded for ![](images/23/23f355a7475101ff2d8f72842b5c291fcddc7b934d9e6a05c63b71c50443a334.svg) although it is unbounded if ![](images/70/707bb132def3690d81bf1f0c8cf416c1382322ab19d66264cdab1decc4669307.svg) is allowed to approach ![](images/8e/8ef8c99c128deb7895aefe6d1a662021e675d3609017391dd57526f775a30207.svg)

- If ![](images/ba/ba33162d712db6f36bcf09e725d626c399881e98edb06cdc4ddfd17532b06701.svg) then ![](images/88/88318ea5b5d7fde77eace946e939b02b531330ff006ea20c887ea2f654acbdf9.svg) for all ![](images/a9/a90dc11635a0cfd7e959687183800180490f43955de346f70950a5720cd92df4.svg) So, trajectories are *bounded*, and we have an *ellipse*.

Let's see some concrete examples." :tutorial/id #uuid "2a925aab-4f30-57a3-a3a2-6c3e21b5b318" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14482 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "7b0e4834-5b7b-5ae6-a7c1-b1def5543b1d" :step/math-academy-id 594290 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167905}} {:db/id 17592186167905 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168010 :tutorial/content "Consider the system of linear differential equations below.

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &=\frac{1}{2}x(t)-4y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t) &=4x(t)+\frac{1}{2}y(t)\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The eigenvalues of the system's matrix are $\lambda_{1,2} = \dfrac{1}{2}\pm4\text{i},$ for which the corresponding eigenvectors are $\mathbf{v}_{1,2} = [\pm \text{i}, 1]^T,$ respectively. Given that the general solution of the system is
![](images/d1/d13abb97b171049a17544fcb312b71d2da3d9294788c1aebe7aa969e99b7819c.svg)
we are interested in sketching the phase portrait of the system of differential equations given above.

If we set $c_1 = 1$ and $c_2 = 0$ in the general solution of the system, we obtain the particular solution:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &={e}^{t/2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) \\ y &={e}^{t/2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Computing the coordinates (rounded to two decimal places) of several points on the curve, we get the table below.

| $t$ | $0$ | $\dfrac{\pi}{16}$ | $\dfrac{\pi}{8}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $x$ | $1$ | $0.78$ | $0$ |
| $y$ | $0$ | $0.78$ | $1.22$ |

Let's sketch this solution in the phase space.

![](images/4f/4f9da4b66977b98b983477d22abb6e00135ea0e1bfa9f785cd0a62d674a7b782.png)

Notice that $|\sin(4t)| \leq 1$ and $|\cos(4t)| \leq 1,$ but $e^{t/2} \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty.$ Thus, the obtained curve is unbounded. So, we have a spiral that is traversed counterclockwise.

Again, since $e^{t/2} \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty,$ the spiral is traversed toward infinity as $t \to \infty.$

The phase portrait of our system looks as follows:
