$$
{lim}_{x\to (-1,1)}\frac{{x}^{2}+xy+x+y}{xy+{y}^{2}}=\frac{(-1)^{2}+(-1)\cdot 1+(-1)+1}{(-1)\cdot 1+{1}^{2}}=\frac{0}{0}
$$

However, we can simplify the limit by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (-1,1)}\frac{{x}^{2}+xy+x+y}{xy+{y}^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to (-1,1)}\frac{x(x+y)+(x+y)}{y(x+y)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (-1,1)}\frac{(x+1)(x+y)}{y(x+y)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (-1,1)}\frac{x+1}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it using direct substitution:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (-1,1)}\frac{x+1}{y} & =\frac{(-1)+1}{1} \\  & =\frac{0}{1} \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $0.$"} :step/id #uuid "5c7e6dac-de5a-50c9-a4a3-207c8cf4283a" :step/next {:db/id 17592186475998}} {:db/id 17592186475997 :step/content {:db/id 17592186345003 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5225a54e-55a7-5758-ada6-d6e76ec121f7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186342920} {:answer/id #uuid "6afe5058-ed29-5490-84ca-cf5ea037f221" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186343150} {:answer/id #uuid "72810408-6a46-5e8d-9beb-52bbe2e8f436" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186343231} {:answer/id #uuid "c186d6e7-0ac4-5259-897c-07e60f6cc561" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186343939} {:answer/id #uuid "fd70e6c7-52f3-50c1-9a16-a6b4b41da448" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186344465}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186343150} :answer-field/id #uuid "c5121edc-c04d-5ea2-9e7a-1a1ca983765e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186344836}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "580ed3de-301a-5585-aa08-af0b5b637cec" :question/math-academy-id "q-74960" :question/problem "${lim}_{x\to (1,1)}\frac{{y}^{2}-x}{\sqrt{x}-y}=$" :question/worked-solution "Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ as follows: 

$$
{lim}_{x\to (1,1)}\frac{{y}^{2}-x}{\sqrt{x}-y}=\frac{{1}^{2}-1}{\sqrt{1}-1}=\frac{0}{0}
$$

However, we can simplify the limit by first multiplying the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1,1)}\frac{{y}^{2}-x}{\sqrt{x}-y} & ={lim}_{x\to (1,1)}\frac{({y}^{2}-x)(\sqrt{x}+y)}{(\sqrt{x}-y)(\sqrt{x}+y)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (1,1)}\frac{({y}^{2}-x)(\sqrt{x}+y)}{{(\sqrt{x})}^{2}-{y}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (1,1)}\frac{-(x-{y}^{2})(\sqrt{x}+y)}{x-{y}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (1,1)}-(\sqrt{x}+y)\end{aligned}
$$

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1,1)}-(\sqrt{x}+y) & =-(\sqrt{1}+1) \\  & =-(1+1) \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $-2.$"} :step/id #uuid "a1d76783-98ca-587b-9e64-3ae5ae7e97c5" :step/next {:db/id 17592186475994}} {:db/id 17592186475998 :step/content {:db/id 17592186475943 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1771b53b-a9ea-5204-9e6c-c3664e7f4eb8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I, II, and III" :db/id 17592186475475} {:answer/id #uuid "52b82999-7d0c-5f60-b09d-5d9bfb9dabdf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II and III only" :db/id 17592186475563} {:answer/id #uuid "644db317-5ce2-5b55-a3a9-b57771242cfe" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II only" :db/id 17592186475590} {:answer/id #uuid "9e112b0b-f642-5793-ba13-d921da5ca298" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186475677} {:answer/id #uuid "d8d267a1-bd0b-57f4-92ed-545ceb83bbea" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and III only" :db/id 17592186475769}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186475475} :answer-field/id #uuid "cbe5df83-a1f1-5212-94d6-8a03a2936996" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186475891}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "83c8f2ad-db17-53f8-868d-e48deabc8feb" :question/math-academy-id "q-129409" :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true regarding the limit given below?

$$
{lim}_{x\to (1,2)}\,\frac{(x-1)(y-2)}{(x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}}
$$

I. The limit evaluates to $0$ along the path $y=2$

II. The limit evaluates to $\frac{1}{2}$ along the path $y=x+1$

III. The limit does not exist" :question/worked-solution "Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1,2)}\,\frac{(x-1)(y-2)}{(x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}} & =\frac{(1-1)(2-2)}{(1-1)^{2}+(2-2)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{0(0)}{{0}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

However, the function cannot be simplified by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

We attempt to evaluate the limit by approaching $(1,2)$ from different paths.

- Statement I is true. Taking $x\to (1,2)$ along the path $y=2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1,2)\,\,\,y=2}\,\frac{(x-1)(y-2)}{(x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\,\frac{(x-1)(2-2)}{(x-1)^{2}+(2-2)^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\,\frac{(x-1)(0)}{(x-1)^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}0 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Taking $x\to (1,2)$ along the path $y=x+1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1,2)\,\,\,y=x+1}\,\frac{(x-1)(y-2)}{(x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{(x-1)(x+1-2)}{(x-1)^{2}+(x+1-2)^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{(x-1)(x-1)}{(x-1)^{2}+(x-1)^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{(x-1)^{2}}{2(x-1)^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{\cancel{(x-1)^{2}}}{2\cancel{(x-1)^{2}}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. Because the limit evaluates to different results on two different paths, we conclude that the limit does not exist:

$$
{lim}_{x\to (1,2)}\,\frac{(x-1)(y-2)}{(x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}}=\text{DNE}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "d56691a3-bd81-5d30-bd36-57d7d11c4bf9"}] :activity/title "Limits and Continuity of Multivariable Functions" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045464 :db/ident :activity.type/review} :db/id 17592186475440} {:db/id 17592186475988 :step/content {:db/id 17592186377695 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3d118fc5-1c52-5566-be98-a9707e774937" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186377697} {:answer/id #uuid "30aa323e-111a-55db-ae16-f96b2c70da3e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186377698} {:answer/id #uuid "563f0bf5-f3be-54dc-b44e-fce9a03892d2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-3" :db/id 17592186377699} {:answer/id #uuid "a81b9d36-0a30-5151-bf36-ec51a5b12490" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186377700} {:answer/id #uuid "f84b3786-3b86-57a7-acce-0bc703bbfb0d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186377701}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186377699} :answer-field/id #uuid "117ca5de-bfde-5504-8e9b-162dc1ee9296" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186377696}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "9d22711b-d1d6-5f06-ab4a-74275f71d77c" :question/math-academy-id "q-74920" :question/problem "Find  ${lim}_{x\to (1,-3)}\frac{xy-y}{x-1}.$" :question/worked-solution "Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ as follows:

$$

$$

$$

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it using direct substitution:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (-1,1)}\frac{x+1}{y} & =\frac{(-1)+1}{1} \\  & =\frac{0}{1} \\  & =0\end{aligned}

:question/math-academy-id "q-129409" :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true regarding the limit given below?

$$
{lim}_{x\to (1,2)}\,\frac{(x-1)(y-2)}{(x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}}
$$

I. The limit evaluates to $0$ along the path $y=2$

II. The limit evaluates to $\frac{1}{2}$ along the path $y=x+1$

III. The limit does not exist" :question/worked-solution "Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1,2)}\,\frac{(x-1)(y-2)}{(x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}} & =\frac{(1-1)(2-2)}{(1-1)^{2}+(2-2)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{0(0)}{{0}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

However, the function cannot be simplified by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

We attempt to evaluate the limit by approaching $(1,2)$ from different paths.

- Statement I is true. Taking $x\to (1,2)$ along the path $y=2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1,2)\,\,\,y=2}\,\frac{(x-1)(y-2)}{(x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\,\frac{(x-1)(2-2)}{(x-1)^{2}+(2-2)^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\,\frac{(x-1)(0)}{(x-1)^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}0 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Taking $x\to (1,2)$ along the path $y=x+1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1,2)\,\,\,y=x+1}\,\frac{(x-1)(y-2)}{(x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{(x-1)(x+1-2)}{(x-1)^{2}+(x+1-2)^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{(x-1)(x-1)}{(x-1)^{2}+(x-1)^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{(x-1)^{2}}{2(x-1)^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{\cancel{(x-1)^{2}}}{2\cancel{(x-1)^{2}}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. Because the limit evaluates to different results on two different paths, we conclude that the limit does not exist:

$$
{lim}_{x\to (1,2)}\,\frac{(x-1)(y-2)}{(x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}}=\text{DNE}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "d56691a3-bd81-5d30-bd36-57d7d11c4bf9"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5225a54e-55a7-5758-ada6-d6e76ec121f7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" $$

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it using direct substitution:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (2,0)}\frac{{y}^{2}-x}{{x}^{3}} & =\frac{{0}^{2}-2}{{2}^{3}} \\  & =-\frac{2}{8} \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}

:question/math-academy-id "q-129401" :question/problem "Determine ${lim}_{x\to (1,0)}\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1}.$" :question/worked-solution "Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1,0)}\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1} & =\frac{{0}^{2}}{{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}-1} \\  & =\frac{0}{1-1} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

However, the function cannot be simplified by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

Let's attempt to evaluate the limit approaching $(1,0)$ from different paths.

- Taking $x\to (1,0)$ along the path $y=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1,0)\,\,\,y=0}\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1} & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{0}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{0}^{2}-1} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}0 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Taking $x\to (1,0)$ along the path $x=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (1,0)\,\,\,x=1}\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1} & ={lim}_{y\to 0}\frac{{y}^{2}}{{1}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1} \\  & ={lim}_{y\to 0}\frac{{y}^{2}}{{y}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{y\to 0}1 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Because the limit evaluates to different results on two different paths, we conclude that the limit does not exist:

$$
{lim}_{x\to (1,0)}\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1}=\text{DNE}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "ee66d94f-00d8-5e5e-84ff-35a7175f7dff"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "154cde04-acab-5465-9547-10829d1c2ac6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2" *predicate* of one variable is a sentence that contains a variable defined on some universal set and has the property that when we substitute a concrete value of the variable into the predicate, the result becomes a mathematical statement that is either true or false.

The **truth set** $T$ of a predicate $P(x)$ is the set of elements in its universal set $U$ such that substituting these elements into the predicate gives a true statement:

$$
T = \big\{ x \in U \: | \: P(x) \big\}
$$

For example, let's find the truth set of the following predicate:

$\qquad$ $D(x):$ $x$ is divisible by $2,$

where the universal set is $U = \big\{ 1,2, \ldots, 6 \big\}.$

To find the truth set $T,$ we need to find $x \in U$ such that the following is true:

$\qquad$ $x$ is divisible by $2.$

Let's check all the elements in our universal set $U$ to determine which of them are elements of the truth set $T{:}$

- $x=1\notin T$ since $1$ is *not* divisible by $2$

- $x=2\in T$ since $2$ is divisible by $2$

- $x=3\notin T$ since $3$ is *not* divisible by $2$

- $x=4\in T$ since $4$ is divisible by $2$

- $x=5\notin T$ since $5$ is *not* divisible by $2$

- $x=6\in T$ since $6$ is divisible by $2$

Therefore, the truth set of our predicate is

$$
T = \big\{ 2,4,6 \big\}.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "8422ca20-ab2c-5e41-a789-3c21465dfc51" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8139 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "dbb18ea5-8c55-58c8-81e5-4c923006baa2" :step/math-academy-id 153521 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199092}} {:db/id 17592186199092 :step/content {:db/id 17592186198279 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186198096 :question/id #uuid "4b253527-f5ca-5927-97f0-d91491d598b3" :question/math-academy-id "e-12721"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "c23caadd-1738-549f-aade-2c983dc250dc" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049002} {:db/id 17592186050035} {:db/id 17592186050073}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186198700} {:db/id 17592186198720} {:db/id 17592186425977} {:db/id 17592186425978}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Truth Set of a Predicate"} :step/id #uuid "3cbfca6e-271d-50e8-8a2d-2854b810036b" :step/math-academy-id 153522 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199093}} {:db/id 17592186199093 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199540 :tutorial/content "A predicate of the variables $x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n$ is a sentence that contains these variables with the property that when we substitute concrete values for all the variables, the result becomes a statement that is either true or false. 

We can denote such a predicate using the following notation:

$$
P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)
$$

If $U_1$ is the universal set for $x_1,U_2$ is the universal set for $x_2,\ldots,$ etc, then the universal set $U$ for our predicate is given by the Cartesian product

$$
U = U_1 \times U_2 \times \cdots \times U_n.
$$

For example, the sentence

$\qquad$ $P(x,y): x+y \lt 2,$ $\quad$ $x,y \in \mathbb{R}$

is a predicate of two variables, $x$ and $y.$ In this case, the universal set is

$$
U = \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R} = \mathbb{R}^2.
$$

The **truth set** $T$ of a predicate $P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$ is the set of $n$-tuples $(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n) \in U$ such that substituting these tuples into the predicate gives a true statement:

$$
T = \big\{ (x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n) \in U \: | \: P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n) \big\}
$$

For example, to determine the truth set of the predicate $P(x,y)$ defined above, we need to find $(x,y) \in \mathbb R^2$ such that the following is true:

$\qquad$ $x+y \lt 2$

To find the truth set, we first find an explicit condition on $y$ as a function of $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}x+y & <2 \\ y & <2-x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the truth set contains all tuples $(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2$ that satisfy this inequality. We can write the truth set $T$ of our predicate as follows:

$$
T = \big\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2 \:|\: y < 2-x\big\}
$$

Finally, since $T$ is a subset of $\mathbb R^2,$ we can represent it as a region in the coordinate plane.

- $x=5\notin T$ since $5$ is *not* divisible by $2$

- $x=6\in T$ since $6$ is divisible by $2$

Therefore, the truth set of our predicate is

$$
T = \big\{ 2,4,6 \big\}.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "8422ca20-ab2c-5e41-a789-3c21465dfc51" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8139 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186199092 :step/content {:db/id 17592186198279 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186198096 :question/id #uuid "4b253527-f5ca-5927-97f0-d91491d598b3" :question/math-academy-id "e-12721"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "c23caadd-1738-549f-aade-2c983dc250dc" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049002} {:db/id 17592186050035} {:db/id 17592186050073}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186198700} {:db/id 17592186198720} {:db/id 17592186425977} {:db/id 17592186425978}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Truth Set of a Predicate"} :step/id #uuid "3cbfca6e-271d-50e8-8a2d-2854b810036b" :step/math-academy-id 153522 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199093}} {:db/id 17592186199093 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199540 :tutorial/content "A predicate of the variables $x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n$ is a sentence that contains these variables with the property that when we substitute concrete values for all the variables, the result becomes a statement that is either true or false. 

We can denote such a predicate using the following notation:

$$
P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)
$$

If $U_1$ is the universal set for $x_1,U_2$ is the universal set for $x_2,\ldots,$ etc, then the universal set $U$ for our predicate is given by the Cartesian product

$$
U = U_1 \times U_2 \times \cdots \times U_n.
$$

For example, the sentence

$\qquad$ $P(x,y): x+y \lt 2,$ $\quad$ $x,y \in \mathbb{R}$

is a predicate of two variables, $x$ and $y.$ In this case, the universal set is

$$
U = \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R} = \mathbb{R}^2.
$$

The **truth set** $T$ of a predicate $P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$ is the set of $n$-tuples $(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n) \in U$ such that substituting these tuples into the predicate gives a true statement:

$$
T = \big\{ (x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n) \in U \: | \: P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n) \big\}
$$

For example, to determine the truth set of the predicate $P(x,y)$ defined above, we need to find $(x,y) \in \mathbb R^2$ such that the following is true:

$\qquad$ $x+y \lt 2$

To find the truth set, we first find an explicit condition on $y$ as a function of $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}x+y & <2 \\ y & <2-x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the truth set contains all tuples $(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2$ that satisfy this inequality. We can write the truth set $T$ of our predicate as follows:

$$
T = \big\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2 \:|\: y < 2-x\big\}
$$

Finally, since $T$ is a subset of $\mathbb R^2,$ we can represent it as a region in the coordinate plane.

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} &=4{b}_{1}+{b}_{2} \\ {c}_{2} &=2{b}_{1}.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

First, we express the $b$'s in terms of $c$'s. From the second equation, we get 

$$
{b}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}{c}_{2}.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
{c}_{1}=4(\frac{1}{2}{c}_{2})+{b}_{2}\,⟹\,{b}_{2}={c}_{1}-2{c}_{2}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={b}_{1}-7{b}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{c}_{2}-7({c}_{1}-2{c}_{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{c}_{2}-7{c}_{1}+14{c}_{2} \\  & =-7{c}_{1}+\frac{29}{2}{c}_{1}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

First, we express the $b$'s in terms of $c$'s. From the first equation, we get 

$$
{b}_{2}=-\frac{1}{2}{c}_{1}.
$$

Substituting this into the second equation, we obtain

$$
{c}_{2}=-2{b}_{1}+(-\frac{1}{2}{c}_{1})\,⟹\,{b}_{1}=-\frac{1}{4}{c}_{1}-\frac{1}{2}{c}_{2}.
$$

Since $[x]_{B}=\begin{bmatrix}-8 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}$, we can write the vector $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =-8{b}_{1}+6{b}_{2} \\  & =-8(-\frac{1}{4}{c}_{1}-\frac{1}{2}{c}_{2})+6(-\frac{1}{2}{c}_{1}) \\  & =2{c}_{1}+4{c}_{2}-3{c}_{1} \\  & =-{c}_{1}+4{c}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

are **disjoint** if they have no element in common. In other words, their intersection is empty:

$$
A \cap B = \emptyset
$$

For example, consider the following sets:

$$
A = \{ -1,-2,-3 \}, \qquad B=\{ 5,10 \}
$$

 

These sets are disjoint since their intersection is empty:

$$
A\cap B = \{ -1,-2,-3 \} \cap \{ 5,10 \} = \emptyset
$$

On the other hand, $C=(-\infty,5]$ and $D=(-2,\infty)$ are *not* disjoint since the intersection of these sets is *not* empty:

$$
C\cap D = (-\infty,5] \cap (-2,\infty) = (-2,5] \neq \emptyset

We'll use the special symbol "$\sqcup$" (square cup) to denote the disjoint union. 

The disjoint union of two non-overlapping (disjoint) sets $A$ and $B$ is simply the union of the sets.

For example, since 

$$
\{ 0,2,4 \} \cap \{ 1, 3 \} = \emptyset,
$$

we find the disjoint union of these sets as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{0,2,4\}⊔\{1,3\} & =\{0,2,4\}\cup \{1,3\} \\  & =\{0,1,2,3,4\}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "4d264ae6-080d-5ca0-be06-b6d41a5f4aa7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8005 :tutorial/title "The Disjoint Union of Non-Overlapping Sets"} :step/id #uuid "a0fe9f92-abdf-5afd-94bd-7e0416495b3f" :step/math-academy-id 157023 :step/next {:db/id 17592186152973}} {:db/id 17592186152973 :step/content {:db/id 17592186152102 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186151818 :question/id #uuid "ea87c6f2-d0ef-5f8d-8f87-b9219272cedd" :question/math-academy-id "e-12761"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "7079378e-2cec-550d-a647-405a0acb9b61" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048899}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186152461} {:db/id 17592186152462} {:db/id 17592186374296} {:db/id 17592186374303} {:db/id 17592186374310} {:db/id 17592186374317} {:db/id 17592186425786} {:db/id 17592186425787}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Disjoint Union of Non-Overlapping Sets"} :step/id #uuid "7342dbf9-8375-507b-9fcc-03ddc4dd27a7" :step/math-academy-id 157024 :step/next {:db/id 17592186152974}} {:db/id 17592186152974 :step/content {:db/id 17592186153436 :tutorial/content "Now, consider the following overlapping sets: 

$$
A_1 = \{ \square, \triangle \}, \qquad A_2 = \{ \heartsuit, \square\}.
$$

These sets overlap because their intersection is non-empty. 

$$
A_1 \cap A_2 = \{ \square \} \neq \emptyset.
$$

To construct the disjoint union of these overlapping sets, we proceed as follows:

- For each of our sets, we form the associated set, where each element is "tagged" with the corresponding index:

$$
\begin{aligned} & {A}_{1} &  & \,\to \, &  & {A}_{1}^{∗}=\{(◻,1),(△,1)\} \\  & {A}_{2} &  & \,\to \, &  & {A}_{2}^{∗}=\{(♡,2),(◻,2)\}\end{aligned}
$$

- As a result, the new sets $A_1^\ast$ and $A_2^\ast$ are non-overlapping. So, the disjoint union of our sets is simply the union of the associated tagged sets:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1}⊔{A}_{2} & =\{◻,△\}⊔\{♡,◻\} \\  & ={A}_{1}^{∗}\cup {A}_{2}^{∗} \\  & =\{(◻,1),(△,1)\}\cup \{(♡,2),(◻,2)\} \\  & =\{(◻,1),(△,1),(♡,2),(◻,2)\}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1e3b30b0-95ac-5b38-a7e6-169cc3409776" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8137 :tutorial/title "The Disjoint Union of Overlapping Sets"} :step/id #uuid "233824ca-a0f9-5e23-af03-ba0c108fc90c" :step/math-academy-id 157027 :step/next {:db/id 17592186152975}} {:db/id 17592186152975 :step/content {:db/id 17592186152103 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186151819 :question/id #uuid "65852684-d9ce-5830-b95f-9abae3dadd4a" :question/math-academy-id "e-12762"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "4c5188a6-60a0-5e38-9164-201c3eb60cd5" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186152463} {:db/id 17592186152464} {:db/id 17592186374324} {:db/id 17592186374331} {:db/id 17592186374338} {:db/id 17592186374345} {:db/id 17592186374352} {:db/id 17592186376164} {:db/id 17592186425785} {:db/id 17592186425788}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Disjoint Union of Overlapping Sets"} :step/id #uuid "d572a9fc-16a3-5783-b7e1-a3d5a6eab501" :step/math-academy-id 157028}] :activity/title "Disjoint Sets" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186152373} {:db/id 17592186152970 :step/content {:db/id 17592186153433 :tutorial/content "Two sets $A$ and $B$ are **disjoint** if they have no element in common. We'll use the special symbol "$\sqcup$" (square cup) to denote the disjoint union. 

The disjoint union of two non-overlapping (disjoint) sets $A$ and $B$ is simply the union of the sets.

$$

$$

we find the disjoint union of these sets as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{0,2,4\}⊔\{1,3\} & =\{0,2,4\}\cup \{1,3\} \\  & =\{0,1,2,3,4\}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "4d264ae6-080d-5ca0-be06-b6d41a5f4aa7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8005 :tutorial/title "The Disjoint Union of Non-Overlapping Sets"} :step/id #uuid "a0fe9f92-abdf-5afd-94bd-7e0416495b3f" :step/math-academy-id 157023 :step/next {:db/id 17592186152973}} {:db/id 17592186153434 :tutorial/content "The **disjoint union** of two sets is defined differently depending on whether the sets are non-overlapping (disjoint) or overlapping (have a non-empty intersection). $$
A_1 = \{ \square, \triangle \}, \qquad A_2 = \{ \heartsuit, \square\}.
$$

These sets overlap because their intersection is non-empty. 

$$
A_1 \cap A_2 = \{ \square \} \neq \emptyset.
$$

To construct the disjoint union of these overlapping sets, we proceed as follows:

- For each of our sets, we form the associated set, where each element is "tagged" with the corresponding index:

$$
\begin{aligned} & {A}_{1} &  & \,\to \, &  & {A}_{1}^{∗}=\{(◻,1),(△,1)\} \\  & {A}_{2} &  & \,\to \, &  & {A}_{2}^{∗}=\{(♡,2),(◻,2)\}\end{aligned}
$$

- As a result, the new sets $A_1^\ast$ and $A_2^\ast$ are non-overlapping. So, the disjoint union of our sets is simply the union of the associated tagged sets:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1}⊔{A}_{2} & =\{◻,△\}⊔\{♡,◻\} \\  & ={A}_{1}^{∗}\cup {A}_{2}^{∗} \\  & =\{(◻,1),(△,1)\}\cup \{(♡,2),(◻,2)\} \\  & =\{(◻,1),(△,1),(♡,2),(◻,2)\}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1e3b30b0-95ac-5b38-a7e6-169cc3409776" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8137 :tutorial/title "The Disjoint Union of Overlapping Sets"} :step/id #uuid "233824ca-a0f9-5e23-af03-ba0c108fc90c" :step/math-academy-id 157027 :step/next {:db/id 17592186152975}} {:db/id 17592186153436 :tutorial/content "Now, consider the following overlapping sets:

In this lesson, we will formally define what we mean by a **vector space.**

First, let $V$ be a set equipped with the following two operations:

Vector addition: 

For any two elements $\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \in V,$ there is a unique element $\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y}$ that also lies in $V.$ We say that $V$ is **closed under vector addition.**

Scalar multiplication: 

For any element $\mathbf{x} \in V$ and any number $\alpha \in \mathbb{R},$ there is a unique element $\alpha \mathbf{x}$ that also lies in $V.$ We say that $V$ is **closed under scalar multiplication.**

A set $V$ equipped with vector addition and scalar multiplication forms a **vector space** if it satisfies the following **vector space axioms**. 

Axioms of Vector Addition ($+$)

- $\color{black}\textrm{[A1]}$: $\color{blue}\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y} =  \mathbf{y}+\mathbf{x}$ for any $\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \in V$; vector addition is **commutative**.

- $\color{black}\textrm{[A2]}$: $\color{blue}(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y})+\mathbf{z} =  \mathbf{x}+(\mathbf{y}+\mathbf{z})$ for any $\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}, \mathbf{z} \in V$; vectors addition is **associative**.

- $\color{black}\textrm{[A3]}$: There exists a **zero-vector** $\mathbf{0}$ such that $\color{blue}\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{0} = \mathbf{x}$.

- $\color{black}\textrm{[A4]}$: For every $\mathbf{x} \in V,$ there exists $-\mathbf{x} \in V$ such that $\color{blue}\mathbf{x} + (-\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{0}$; $-\mathbf{x}$ is called the **negative** of $\mathbf{x}$.

Axioms of Scalar Multiplication ($\cdot$)

- $\color{black}\textrm{[A5]}$: $\color{blue}1 \cdot \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{x}$ for any $\mathbf{x} \in V$; multiplying by $1$ does not change a vector.

- $\color{black}\textrm{[A6]}$: $\color{blue}\alpha (\beta \mathbf{x}) = (\alpha\beta) \mathbf{x}$ for any numbers $\alpha,\beta \in \mathbb{R}$ and any vector $\mathbf{x} \in V$.

Axioms Connecting Vector Addition and Scalar Multiplication (the Distributive Laws)

- $\color{black}\textrm{[A7]}$: $\color{blue}(\alpha + \beta)\mathbf{x} = \alpha \mathbf{x} + \beta \mathbf{x}$ for any numbers $\alpha,\beta \in \mathbb{R}$ and any vector $\mathbf{x} \in V$.

- $\color{black}\textrm{[A8]}$: $\color{blue}\alpha (\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{y}) = \alpha \mathbf{x} + \alpha \mathbf{y}$ for any number $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ and any vectors $\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \in V$.

So, a vector space is simply a collective term for all kinds of sets equipped with addition and scalar multiplication, where these operations satisfy this particular list of axioms (which are similar to the properties of these operations in $\mathbb{R}^n$). 

The elements of any vector space are called **vectors**." :tutorial/id #uuid "488db0ee-92f8-5790-8ff6-2977ab0e6dce" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3187 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "From top to bottom, fill in the blanks and hence complete the proof of the following statement using the axioms $[\text{A}1]-[\text{A}8]$ given below.

*Statement: *

*$0\cdot 0=0$* 

*Proof:*

$$
\begin{aligned}0\cdot 0 & =0\cdot 0 &  & [\,\text{given}\,] \\ 0\cdot 0 & =0\cdot 0+0 &  & [\,\text{axiom __}\,\,] \\ 0\cdot 0 & =0\cdot 0+1\cdot 0 &  & [\,\text{axiom __}\,\,] \\ 0\cdot 0 & =(0+1)\cdot 0 &  & [\,\text{axiom A7}\,] \\ 0\cdot 0 & =1\cdot 0 &  & [\,\text{addition of integers}\,] \\ 0\cdot 0 & =0 &  & [\,\text{axiom A5}\,]\end{aligned}
$$

The axioms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{[A1]}:x+y=y+x & \text{[A5]}:1\cdot x=x \\ \text{[A2]}:(x+y)+z=x+(y+z) & \text{[A6]}:\alpha (\beta x)=(\alpha \beta )x \\ \text{[A3]}:x+0=x & \text{[A7]}:(\alpha +\beta )x=\alpha x+\beta x \\ \text{[A4]}:x+(-x)=0 & \text{[A8]}:\alpha (x+y)=\alpha x+\alpha y\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "Using the vector space axioms, we obtain the following:

*$T$ is **not** a vector space (with respect to addition of matrices and multiplication of matrices by a real number) because $\text{____}\,.$*" :question/worked-solution "The correct answer is 

*$T$ is **not** a vector space (with respect to addition of matrices and multiplication of matrices by a real number) because **multiplication by a scalar is not closed.** *

 For example, the identity matrix 

$$

$$

lies in $T$, but

$$

$$

Complete the following sentence:

*$T$ is **not** a vector space (with respect to addition of matrices and multiplication of matrices by a real number) because $\text{____}\,.$*" :question/worked-solution "The correct answer is 

*$T$ is **not** a vector space (with respect to addition of matrices and multiplication of matrices by a real number) because **multiplication by a scalar is not closed.** *

 For example, the identity matrix 

$$
I=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix},
$$

lies in $T$, but

$$
\sqrt{2}\cdot I=\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt{2} & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt{2}\end{bmatrix}\notin T
$$

because $\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{2}$ is not a rational number.

On the other hand,

- The zero matrix belongs to $T.$  $\,✓$

- Addition of matrices with real entries is commutative, in general.    $\,✓$

- Addition of matrices with real entries is associative, in general.    $\,✓$

*If $w$ and $v$ are vectors such that $x+w=v+x$ for some $x\in V$, then $w=v.$*

*Proof:*

$$
\begin{aligned}x+w & =v+x &  & [\,\text{given}\,] \\ (x+w)+(-x) & =(v+x)+(-x) &  & [\,\text{add }-x\text{ to both sides}\,] \\ (w+x)+(-x) & =(v+x)+(-x) &  & [\,\text{axiom __}\,\,] \\ w+(x+(-x)) & =v+(x+(-x)) &  & [\,\text{axiom A2}\,] \\ w+0 & =v+0 &  & [\,\text{axiom __}\,\,] \\ w & =v &  & [\,\text{axiom A3}\,]\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}\text{[A1]}:x+y=y+x & \text{[A5]}:1\cdot x=x \\ \text{[A2]}:(x+y)+z=x+(y+z) & \text{[A6]}:\alpha (\beta x)=(\alpha \beta )x \\ \text{[A3]}:x+0=x & \text{[A7]}:(\alpha +\beta )x=\alpha x+\beta x \\ \text{[A4]}:x+(-x)=0 & \text{[A8]}:\alpha (x+y)=\alpha x+\alpha y\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "Using the vector space axioms, we obtain the following:

*$A$ is **not** a vector space (with respect to function addition and scalar multiplication) because $\text{_________}\,.$*" :question/worked-solution "The correct answer is as follows:

:step/math-academy-id 38121} {:db/id 17592186193681 :step/content {:db/id 17592186193897 :tutorial/content "Likelihood functions of samples drawn from populations modeled using continuous random variables are defined similarly to discrete variables. The only difference is that we use probability density functions instead of probability mass functions.

If $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed *continuous* random variables with probability density function $f(x; \theta),$ then the likelihood function of a random sample $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ is given by

$$
L(\theta) = P(X_1=x_1, X_2=x_2, \ldots , X_n = x_n) = \displaystyle\prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i;\,\theta).
$$

For example, let $X_1, X_2, X_3$ be continuous, I.I.D. random variables with the following probability density function:

$$
f(x; \theta) = \theta x^{-\theta-1}, \qquad x \geq 1
$$

Here, $\theta$ is an unknown parameter. Suppose we conduct our random sample and get the following results:

$$
x_1 = 2.5, \qquad x_2 = 3.2, \qquad x_3 = 1.2.
$$

 

In this case, we compute the likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}L(\theta ) & ={\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\theta {x}_{i}^{-\theta -1}) \\  & =(\theta {x}_{1}^{-\theta -1})\cdot (\theta {x}_{2}^{-\theta -1})⋯(\theta {x}_{n}^{-\theta -1}) \\  & ={\theta }^{n}({x}_{1}^{-\theta -1})\cdot ({x}_{2}^{-\theta -1})⋯({x}_{n}^{-\theta -1}) \\  & ={\theta }^{n}{({x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}⋯{x}_{n})}^{-\theta -1} \\  & ={\theta }^{n}({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i})^{-\theta -1}\end{aligned}
$$

For our sample, we have $n=3$, and

$$
\begin{aligned}{\prod }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i} & =2.5\cdot 3.2\cdot 1.2=9.6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
L(\theta) = \theta^{3} ( 9.6 )^{-\theta-1}.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "5e339526-e303-5047-8def-188a04dca982" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7001 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "7a3131cc-aeb5-5d42-af4a-921157386704" :step/math-academy-id 42268 :step/next {:db/id 17592186193687}} {:db/id 17592186193685 :step/content {:db/id 17592186192797 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186192521 :question/id #uuid "2ff20920-30c5-5027-b461-31b13d2031e5" :question/math-academy-id "e-11121"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "6068f85b-0ea6-5161-a8d1-d4eb2504852b" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050018}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186192985} {:db/id 17592186193195} {:db/id 17592186441777} {:db/id 17592186441783} {:db/id 17592186441784} {:db/id 17592186441785} {:db/id 17592186441787} {:db/id 17592186510388} {:db/id 17592186510408}] :knowledge-point/title "Likelihood Functions for Exponential Random Variables"} :step/id #uuid "9623ba3e-7523-5921-af5c-689ea499d4b4" :step/math-academy-id 42283 :step/next {:db/id 17592186193692}} {:db/id 17592186193687 :step/content {:db/id 17592186192799 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186192523 :question/id #uuid "bd63ff93-762d-5d7d-be8d-9701130b9fe5" :question/math-academy-id "e-11123"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "cbba4fae-4e47-5a69-a6c1-d8754c18767a" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048485} {:db/id 17592186049638}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186192986} {:db/id 17592186193201} {:db/id 17592186441775} {:db/id 17592186441782} {:db/id 17592186441786} {:db/id 17592186441788} {:db/id 17592186510400}] :knowledge-point/title "Likelihood Functions for Continuous Random Variables"} :step/id #uuid "bc09f530-58a5-566a-a408-bd7b51bd761e" :step/math-academy-id 42301 :step/next {:db/id 17592186193685}} {:db/id 17592186193692 :step/content {:db/id 17592186193902 :tutorial/content "The probability density function of a normally distributed random variable $X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ is given by

$$
f(x) = \dfrac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\frac12\left(\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^2}.
$$

Some example normal distribution curves are shown below. 

![](images/c9/c9359fc84401aabb19e526755b70647cb0496fa8ddba65974466e0ffc3dbbbdc.png)

If we set $\sigma=1,$ then $f(x)$ simplifies as follows:

$$
f(x) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-(x-\mu)^2/2}.
$$

This is a standard normal random variable whose mean is shifted right by $\mu$ units.

Finally, setting the unknown parameter as $\theta$ when discussing likelihood functions is common. Following this convention, we set $\mu=\theta,$ and we get

$$
f(x;\theta) =  \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-(x-\theta)^2/2}.
$$

Let's use this to compute some likelihood functions of some normally distributed sample data." :tutorial/id #uuid "8e08170d-c55e-531f-a8b9-99dfa8ecbac7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7019 :tutorial/title "The Normal Distribution"} :step/id #uuid "5912947a-0cd6-5e5a-958c-a4fff1dab140" :step/math-academy-id 42321 :step/next {:db/id 17592186193505}}] :activity/title "Likelihood Functions for Continuous Probability Distributions" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186192932} {:db/id 17592186193681 :step/content {:db/id 17592186193897 :tutorial/content "Likelihood functions of samples drawn from populations modeled using continuous random variables are defined similarly to discrete variables. $$

$$

For example, let $X_1, X_2, X_3$ be continuous, I.I.D. random variables with the following probability density function:

$$

Here, $\theta$ is an unknown parameter. Suppose we conduct our random sample and get the following results:

$$

$$
L(\theta) = \theta^{3} ( 9.6 )^{-\theta-1}.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "5e339526-e303-5047-8def-188a04dca982" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7001 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "7a3131cc-aeb5-5d42-af4a-921157386704" :step/math-academy-id 42268 :step/next {:db/id 17592186193687}} {:db/id 17592186193505 :step/content {:db/id 17592186192684 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186192389 :question/id #uuid "2393d607-0f73-59f3-9a5f-ebe45050dda9" :question/math-academy-id "e-10106"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "d363c839-34b6-55c7-85d8-f2013e08cc62" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048615}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186193196} {:db/id 17592186193197} {:db/id 17592186441776} {:db/id 17592186441778} {:db/id 17592186441779} {:db/id 17592186441780} {:db/id 17592186441781} {:db/id 17592186510380} {:db/id 17592186510401}] :knowledge-point/title "Likelihood Functions for Normal Random Variables"} :step/id #uuid "f15a8c24-10c0-50c8-9701-f1e1122791bf" :step/math-academy-id 38121} {:db/id 17592186193897 :tutorial/content "Likelihood functions of samples drawn from populations modeled using continuous random variables are defined similarly to discrete variables. The only difference is that we use probability density functions instead of probability mass functions.

If $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed *continuous* random variables with probability density function $f(x; \theta),$ then the likelihood function of a random sample $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ is given by

$$
L(\theta) = P(X_1=x_1, X_2=x_2, \ldots , X_n = x_n) = \displaystyle\prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i;\,\theta).
$$

For example, let $X_1, X_2, X_3$ be continuous, I.I.D. random variables with the following probability density function:

$$
f(x; \theta) = \theta x^{-\theta-1}, \qquad x \geq 1
$$

Here, $\theta$ is an unknown parameter. Suppose we conduct our random sample and get the following results:

$$
x_1 = 2.5, \qquad x_2 = 3.2, \qquad x_3 = 1.2.
$$

 

In this case, we compute the likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}L(\theta ) & ={\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\theta {x}_{i}^{-\theta -1}) \\  & =(\theta {x}_{1}^{-\theta -1})\cdot (\theta {x}_{2}^{-\theta -1})⋯(\theta {x}_{n}^{-\theta -1}) \\  & ={\theta }^{n}({x}_{1}^{-\theta -1})\cdot ({x}_{2}^{-\theta -1})⋯({x}_{n}^{-\theta -1}) \\  & ={\theta }^{n}{({x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}⋯{x}_{n})}^{-\theta -1} \\  & ={\theta }^{n}({\prod }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i})^{-\theta -1}\end{aligned}
$$

For our sample, we have $n=3$, and

$$
\begin{aligned}{\prod }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i} & =2.5\cdot 3.2\cdot 1.2=9.6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
L(\theta) = \theta^{3} ( 9.6 )^{-\theta-1}.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "5e339526-e303-5047-8def-188a04dca982" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7001 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186193687 :step/content {:db/id 17592186192799 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186192523 :question/id #uuid "bd63ff93-762d-5d7d-be8d-9701130b9fe5" :question/math-academy-id "e-11123"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "cbba4fae-4e47-5a69-a6c1-d8754c18767a" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048485} {:db/id 17592186049638}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186192986} {:db/id 17592186193201} {:db/id 17592186441775} {:db/id 17592186441782} {:db/id 17592186441786} {:db/id 17592186441788} {:db/id 17592186510400}] :knowledge-point/title "Likelihood Functions for Continuous Random Variables"} :step/id #uuid "bc09f530-58a5-566a-a408-bd7b51bd761e" :step/math-academy-id 42301 :step/next {:db/id 17592186193685}} {:db/id 17592186193685 :step/content {:db/id 17592186192797 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186192521 :question/id #uuid "2ff20920-30c5-5027-b461-31b13d2031e5" :question/math-academy-id "e-11121"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "6068f85b-0ea6-5161-a8d1-d4eb2504852b" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050018}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186192985} {:db/id 17592186193195} {:db/id 17592186441777} {:db/id 17592186441783} {:db/id 17592186441784} {:db/id 17592186441785} {:db/id 17592186441787} {:db/id 17592186510388} {:db/id 17592186510408}] :knowledge-point/title "Likelihood Functions for Exponential Random Variables"} :step/id #uuid "9623ba3e-7523-5921-af5c-689ea499d4b4" :step/math-academy-id 42283 :step/next {:db/id 17592186193692}} {:db/id 17592186193692 :step/content {:db/id 17592186193902 :tutorial/content "The probability density function of a normally distributed random variable $X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ is given by

$$
f(x) = \dfrac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\frac12\left(\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^2}.
$$

Some example normal distribution curves are shown below. 

![](images/c9/c9359fc84401aabb19e526755b70647cb0496fa8ddba65974466e0ffc3dbbbdc.png)

If we set $\sigma=1,$ then $f(x)$ simplifies as follows:

$$
f(x) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-(x-\mu)^2/2}.
$$

This is a standard normal random variable whose mean is shifted right by $\mu$ units.

Finally, setting the unknown parameter as $\theta$ when discussing likelihood functions is common. Following this convention, we set $\mu=\theta,$ and we get

$$
f(x;\theta) =  \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-(x-\theta)^2/2}.
$$

Let's use this to compute some likelihood functions of some normally distributed sample data." :tutorial/id #uuid "8e08170d-c55e-531f-a8b9-99dfa8ecbac7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7019 :tutorial/title "The Normal Distribution"} :step/id #uuid "5912947a-0cd6-5e5a-958c-a4fff1dab140" :step/math-academy-id 42321 :step/next {:db/id 17592186193505}} {:db/id 17592186193902 :tutorial/content "The probability density function of a normally distributed random variable $X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ is given by

:question/math-academy-id "q-159874" :question/problem "Suppose ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{5}$ is an I.I.D random sample with ${X}_{i}∼\text{Exp}(\theta )$ and unknown rate parameter $\theta .$ For a $$

Find the likelihood function of the sample.

$$

Given that the likelihood function of the sample $0.3,\,1.2,\,-2.6,\,0.4$ is

$$
L(\theta )=\frac{1}{4{\pi }^{2}}\,{e}^{\,g(\theta )},
$$

what is the expression for $g(\theta )?$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed continuous random variables with probability density function $f(x;\theta ),$ where $\theta $ is an unknown parameter, then the likelihood function of a random sample ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}$ is

$$
L(\theta )=P({X}_{1}={x}_{1},{X}_{2}={x}_{2},…,{X}_{n}={x}_{n})={\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i};\,\theta ).
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=4$ independent normal random variables with unknown mean $\theta $ and variance ${\sigma }^{2}=1,$ for which the probability density function is

$$
f(x;\theta )=\frac{1}{\sigma \sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-\frac{1}{2}{(\frac{x-\theta }{\sigma })}^{2}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2},\,x\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

We can calculate the likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}L(\theta ) & ={\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-({x}_{i}-\theta )^{2}/2}) \\  & =(2\pi )^{-n/2}\,{e}^{-\sum ({x}_{i}-\theta )^{2}/2} \\  & =(2\pi )^{-n/2}\,{e}^{-(\sum {x}_{i}^{2}-2\theta \sum {x}_{i}+n{\theta }^{2})/2} \\  & =(2\pi )^{-n/2}\,{e}^{-(C-2S\theta +n{\theta }^{2})/2}\end{aligned}
$$

where $S={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}$ and $C={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}^{2}.$

For our sample, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}S & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i} \\  & =0.3+1.2+(-2.6)+0.4 \\  & =-0.7 \\ C & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}^{2} \\  & =(0.3)^{2}+(1.2)^{2}+(-2.6)^{2}+(0.4)^{2} \\  & =8.45\end{aligned}
$$

and $n=4.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}L(\theta ) & =(2\pi )^{-4/2}\,{e}^{-(8.45-2(-0.7)\theta +4{\theta }^{2})/2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4{\pi }^{2}}\,{e}^{\,-4.225\,-\,0.7\theta \,-\,2{\theta }^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
g(\theta )=-4.225-0.7\theta -2{\theta }^{2}.

17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "67f89f72-de60-5983-9ba7-f68316fa9c35" :question/math-academy-id "q-159972" :question/problem "Suppose ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},{X}_{3},{X}_{4}$ is an I.I.D random sample with ${X}_{i}∼N(\theta ,1),$  where $\theta $ is an unknown mean.  Given that the likelihood function of the sample $0.3,\,1.2,\,-2.6,\,0.4$ is

$$
L(\theta )=\frac{1}{4{\pi }^{2}}\,{e}^{\,g(\theta )},
$$

what is the expression for $g(\theta )?$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed continuous random variables with probability density function $f(x;\theta ),$ where $\theta $ is an unknown parameter, then the likelihood function of a random sample ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}$ is

$$
L(\theta )=P({X}_{1}={x}_{1},{X}_{2}={x}_{2},…,{X}_{n}={x}_{n})={\prod }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i};\,\theta ).
$$

In our case, we are given a sample of $n=4$ independent normal random variables with unknown mean $\theta $ and variance ${\sigma }^{2}=1,$ for which the probability density function is

$$
f(x;\theta )=\frac{1}{\sigma \sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-\frac{1}{2}{(\frac{x-\theta }{\sigma })}^{2}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-(x-\theta )^{2}/2},\,x\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

We can calculate the likelihood function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}L(\theta ) & ={\prod }_{i=1}^{n}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{e}^{-({x}_{i}-\theta )^{2}/2}) \\  & =(2\pi )^{-n/2}\,{e}^{-\sum ({x}_{i}-\theta )^{2}/2} \\  & =(2\pi )^{-n/2}\,{e}^{-(\sum {x}_{i}^{2}-2\theta \sum {x}_{i}+n{\theta }^{2})/2} \\  & =(2\pi )^{-n/2}\,{e}^{-(C-2S\theta +n{\theta }^{2})/2}\end{aligned}
$$

where $S={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}$ and $C={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}^{2}.$

For our sample, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}S & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i} \\  & =0.3+1.2+(-2.6)+0.4 \\  & =-0.7 \\ C & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}^{2} \\  & =(0.3)^{2}+(1.2)^{2}+(-2.6)^{2}+(0.4)^{2} \\  & =8.45\end{aligned}
$$

and $n=4.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}L(\theta ) & =(2\pi )^{-4/2}\,{e}^{-(8.45-2(-0.7)\theta +4{\theta }^{2})/2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4{\pi }^{2}}\,{e}^{\,-4.225\,-\,0.7\theta \,-\,2{\theta }^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
g(\theta )=-4.225-0.7\theta -2{\theta }^{2}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "9adaeb98-58da-5087-9e4e-fb6fed2b0b66"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "09c1d491-402e-555e-a666-7f7c4e87d6ba" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value domain. Now, we'll learn how to define a double integral over a non-rectangular region.

Let's consider the non-rectangular region $D$ enclosed by the circle $x^2+y^2=1$ in the first quadrant, as shown below. 

![](images/e8/e80bcbaff16282f00e7e3df487d78cfbc51bb2e9660dde5e2fc421cd4d70a9af.png)

 

We will define the following double integral over this non-rectangular region:

$$
\iint\limits_{D} (3-x^2-2y^2) \, \textrm{d}A
$$

To do this, we will use the following trick. Let's enclose the region $D$ by a rectangle $R$ with sides parallel to the coordinates axes, as shown below. 

![](images/21/214db95d949a8658e3fdbfea8f54c0e3bf914c11d9ef88e1ca4264d64d360c90.png)

 

Now, we extend our function to $R$ by setting a new function $f(x,y)$ that's equal to $0$ outside $D$ and equals $3-x^2-2y^2$ on $D\mathbin{:}$

![](images/ab/ab8eed93d71415d810f4c8c9b19d690317769e270805a6925d35f5f0e4c9671f.svg)

![](images/43/43288ccc496832a1a78f9fcaaabb4a5841fc79db5d2082dff7d4177005b61d01.png)

 

Although $f(x,y)$ might not be continuous at the boundary of $D,$ the double integral of $f(x,y)$ over the rectangular domain $R$ will exist. 

Therefore, we define our double integral of $3-x^2-2y^2$ over $D$ as 

$$
\iint\limits_D (3-x^2-2y^2) \, \textrm{d}A = \iint\limits_R f(x,y) \, \textrm{d}A.
$$

Geometrically, the value of the double integral will give us the volume of the solid bounded by the surface $z=3-x^2-2y^2$ over the quarter-circular domain $D.$

**Watch out!** The domain $R$ must not necessarily be the smallest possible rectangle that covers the region $D.$ It can be any rectangular domain that covers $D$ completely." :tutorial/id #uuid $$

which of the following could be the definition of the rectangular domain $R?$

I. $R=[-1,1]\times [-1,1]$

III. $R=[-2,2]\times [-2,2]$

Notice that if $R$ covers $D$ completely and we define 

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y), & (x,y)\in R\cap D \\ 0, & (x,y)\in R∖D,\end{aligned}
$$

we obtain

$$
{∬}_{D}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)\,\text{d}A={∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine each of the given rectangles.

- Rectangle II does not cover the region $D.$

$$

$$

With that in mind, let's examine each of the given functions.

$$
\iint\limits_S \,  \text{d}S = \iint\limits_D \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial x}{\partial y}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial x}{\partial z}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
x = y+\sqrt 2 z, \qquad (y,z)\in D,
$$

where 

$$
D = \big\{ (y,z) \: : \: 1 \leq y \leq 2, \: 1 \leq z \leq 3\big\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/24/240ac546b0dd725e392dd0bd475b2ef00eebce2594be5921285e227137538c46.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y+\sqrt{2}z)=1, \\ \frac{∂x}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(y+\sqrt{2}z)=\sqrt{2},\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂x}{∂y})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂x}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(1)}^{2}+{(\sqrt{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{4}\,\text{d}A \\  & =2{∬}_{D}\,\text{d}A \\  & =2\cdot \text{Area}(D) \\  & =2\cdot (2-1)\cdot (3-1) \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186176213 :question/id #uuid "8af4bd3c-88f6-5bab-b3f1-d47b821bfa03" :question/math-academy-id "q-106023"} {:db/id 17592186176214 :question/id #uuid the $xz$-plane is bounded by $z=\sqrt{x},$ $x=4,$ and the $x$-axis." :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ defined by $y=f(x,z)$ with $(x,z)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂y}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂y}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
y=\frac{4}{7}{x}^{7/4}+z,\,(x,z)\in D,
$$

where 

$$
D={(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 4,\,0\le z\le \sqrt{x}},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/0a/0a4ed826b683e7e8d8ed3e05bcb75618e74314febcdda8ae31b09f379ca21c73.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂y}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{4}{7}{x}^{7/4}+z)={x}^{3/4}, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\frac{4}{7}{x}^{7/4}+z)=1,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂y}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂y}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{({x}^{3/4})}^{2}+(1)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{2+{x}^{3/2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{x}}\sqrt{2+{x}^{3/2}}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}\sqrt{2+{x}^{3/2}}\cdot z\,{|}_{z=0}^{z=\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}\sqrt{2+{x}^{3/2}}\cdot \sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting $u=2+{x}^{3/2},$ we get $\text{d}u=\frac{3}{2}\sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x.$ Also, the limits must be changed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & 0 & 4 \\ u & 2 & 10\end{aligned}
$$

 

Substituting these into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{4}\sqrt{2+{x}^{3/2}}\cdot \sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{2}^{10}\frac{2}{3}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{4}{9}{u}^{3/2}\,{|}_{2}^{10} \\  & =\frac{4}{9}({10}^{3/2}-{2}^{3/2}) \\  & =\frac{4}{9}(10\sqrt{10}-2\sqrt{2}) \\  & =\frac{8\sqrt{2}}{9}(5\sqrt{5}-1).\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186278428 :question/id #uuid "1d826d14-2298-585c-90fc-f27a43f9e900" :question/math-academy-id "q-161213"} {:db/id 17592186278429 :question/id #uuid :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ defined by $x=f(y,z)$ with $(y,z)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂x}{∂y})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂x}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
x={e}^{y}-z,\,(y,z)\in D,
$$

where 

$$
D={(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le \frac{1}{2},\,0\le z\le {e}^{2y}},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/9c/9cae5b68f77c2d79df8a81d0421146ac2bbe618c6065a457c33c86caceeb1327.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{y}-z)={e}^{y}, \\ \frac{∂x}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({e}^{y}-z)=-1,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂x}{∂y})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂x}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+({e}^{y})^{2}+(-1)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{{e}^{2y}+2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1/2}{\int }_{0}^{{e}^{2y}}\sqrt{{e}^{2y}+2}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1/2}\sqrt{{e}^{2y}+2}\cdot z\,{|}_{z=0}^{z={e}^{2y}}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1/2}\sqrt{{e}^{2y}+2}\cdot {e}^{2y}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting $u={e}^{2y}+2,$ we get $\text{d}u=2{e}^{2y}\,\text{d}y.$ Also, the limits must be changed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & 0 & 1/2 \\ u & 3 & e+2\end{aligned}
$$

 

Substituting these into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1/2}\sqrt{{e}^{2y}+2}\cdot {e}^{2y}\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{3}^{e+2}\frac{1}{2}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{u}^{3/2}\,{|}_{3}^{e+2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}((e+2)^{3/2}-{3}^{3/2}) \\  & =\frac{(e+2)^{3/2}-3\sqrt{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186278435 :question/id #uuid "1e867d73-e633-518f-b45d-26ad639d5221" :question/math-academy-id "q-161230"} {:db/id 17592186278511 :question/id #uuid and $0\le y\le 2.$" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
z=\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}},\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 2.
$$

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}})=-\frac{x}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}}, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}})=0,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(-\frac{x}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}})^{2}+(0)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+\frac{{x}^{2}}{4-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{\frac{4}{4-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{2}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}}\cdot y\,{|}_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{2\sqrt{1-\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{(\frac{x}{2})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting $u=\frac{x}{2},$ we get $\text{d}u=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}x.$ Also, the limits must be changed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & 0 & 1 \\ u & 0 & \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Substituting these into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{(\frac{x}{2})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =2{\int }_{0}^{1/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot 2\text{d}u \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{1/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =4\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u\,{|}_{0}^{1/2} \\  & =4(\frac{\pi }{6}-0) \\  & =\frac{2\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186415940 :question/id #uuid "795a5978-6945-51dd-9230-522e60fb9dd8" :question/math-academy-id "q-161129"} {:db/id 17592186415942 :question/id #uuid "Find the surface area of the portion of the plane $z = 2y+2x$ whose projection onto the $xy$-plane is bounded by $y=\cos{x}$ and the $x$-axis from $x=0$ to $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}.$" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \,  \text{d}S = \iint\limits_D \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
z = 2y+2x, \qquad (x,y)\in D,
$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D = \left\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \: 0 \leq y \leq \cos{x} \right\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/e7/e74d609a1288446f0f3adc0de65b814f2a6daaf2d398478e7834882f3be68c8c.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2y+2x)=2, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y+2x)=2,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(2)^{2}+(2)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}3\,\text{d}A \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}y\,{|}_{0}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =3(1-0) \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186049997} {:db/id 17592186176212 :question/id #uuid "e4db5214-9bc0-5164-942e-d1880ba6e86c" :question/math-academy-id "q-106000"} {:db/id 17592186176243 :question/id #uuid "2966982a-a726-53e7-923f-2ca43760b756" :knowledge-point/title "Changing to Polar Coordinates"}] :question/problem "Find the surface area of the part of the cone $z=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ that is subject to the constraints  $x^2 + y^2 \leq 4,\, x\geq 0$ and $y\geq 0.$" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \,  \text{d}S = \iint\limits_D \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
z = \sqrt{x^2+y^2}, \qquad (x,y)\in D,
$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: x^2+y^2\leq 4, \, x\geq 0, \, y\geq 0 \big\},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/be/be8246dc3bfe1bf16af5d9913fc4e6aef58ddad282646a00d3e31120f6bf31e8.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}})=\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}})=\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}},\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}})}^{2}+{(\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+\frac{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

In polar coordinates $(r, \theta),$ the region $D$ can be expressed as 

$$
\Delta = \left\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: 0 \leq r \leq 2, \: 0 \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\sqrt{2}\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{2}r\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\,\text{d}\theta {\int }_{0}^{2}r\,\text{d}r \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot [\theta ]_{0}^{\pi /2}\cdot {[\frac{{r}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{\pi }{2}\cdot 2 \\  & =\pi \sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186176248 :question/id #uuid "29d4c247-c6fe-5732-b0d8-fc8ae1646f2f" :question/math-academy-id "q-109763"} {:db/id 17592186176395 :question/id #uuid ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 9$ and $x\le 0.$" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
z=2y-x,\,(x,y)\in D
$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 9,\,x\le 0},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/3c/3c6c556ec90138fa1f0b599c6afed9d093e5c1b10f7751a5fbe55f0add617e1d.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2y-x)=-1, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y-x)=2,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(-1)^{2}+(2)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+1+4}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{6}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region $D$ can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 3,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{2}}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\sqrt{6}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\sqrt{6}\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{6}\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{6}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}\,\text{d}\theta {\int }_{0}^{3}r\,\text{d}r \\  & =\sqrt{6}\cdot [\theta ]_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}\cdot {[\frac{{r}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =\sqrt{6}\cdot \pi \cdot \frac{9}{2} \\  & =\frac{9\pi \sqrt{6}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186278405 :question/id #uuid "95ffc39b-753c-5fd6-923e-0b13c7adc887" :question/math-academy-id "q-161165"} {:db/id 17592186278406 :question/id #uuid hemisphere $z=\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}$ that is subject to the constraints ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 1$ and $y\ge 0.$" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
z=\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}},\,(x,y)\in D
$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 1,\,y\ge 0},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/e7/e7cb4d16f39d1c1e38d65000471cbc5ca1831a0bbc2cfc61c4f03d087d6a5125.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}})=-\frac{x}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}})=-\frac{y}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}},\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(-\frac{x}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}})}^{2}+{(-\frac{y}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+\frac{{x}^{2}}{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{\frac{4}{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{2}{\sqrt{4-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region $D$ can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 1,\,0\le \theta \le \pi }.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{2}{\sqrt{4-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{2}{\sqrt{4-{r}^{2}}}\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{2r}{\sqrt{4-{r}^{2}}}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\,\text{d}\theta {\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{2r}{\sqrt{4-{r}^{2}}}\,\text{d}r \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{2r}{\sqrt{4-{r}^{2}}}\,\text{d}r.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting $u=4-{r}^{2},$ we get $\text{d}u=-2r\,\text{d}r.$ Also, the limits must be changed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & 0 & 1 \\ u & 4 & 3\end{aligned}
$$

 

Substituting these into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{2r}{\sqrt{4-{r}^{2}}}\,\text{d}r & =-\pi {\int }_{4}^{3}\frac{1}{\sqrt{u}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\pi {\int }_{3}^{4}{u}^{-1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\pi \cdot 2{({u}^{1/2})}_{3}^{4} \\  & =2\pi \cdot ({4}^{1/2}-{3}^{1/2}) \\  & =2\pi (2-\sqrt{3}).\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186278407 :question/id #uuid "b5e36073-07ed-5be9-b9f9-14a5dbeadf43" :question/math-academy-id "q-161173" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186176065 :knowledge-point/id #uuid to the constraints ${y}^{2}+{z}^{2}\le 9$ and $z\le 0.$" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ defined by $x=f(y,z)$ with $(y,z)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂x}{∂y})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂x}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
x={z}^{2}-{y}^{2},\,(y,z)\in D
$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D={(y,z)\,:\,{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}\le 9,\,z\le 0},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/cd/cd5bcd7857769afb5f3a4f6197757c08eb295c7075a271c302c4b6087d661d14.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({z}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2y, \\ \frac{∂x}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({z}^{2}-{y}^{2})=2z,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂x}{∂y})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂x}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(-2y)^{2}+(2z)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4{y}^{2}+4{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4({y}^{2}+{z}^{2})}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region $D$ can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 3,\,\pi \le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4({y}^{2}+{z}^{2})}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta {\int }_{0}^{3}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting $u=1+4{r}^{2},$ we get $\text{d}u=8r\,\text{d}r.$ Also, the limits must be changed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & 0 & 3 \\ u & 1 & 37\end{aligned}
$$

 

Substituting these into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r & =\pi \cdot \frac{1}{8}{\int }_{1}^{37}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\pi }{8}{\int }_{1}^{37}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\pi }{8}\cdot \frac{2}{3}{[{u}^{3/2}]}_{1}^{37} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{12}{[{u}^{3/2}]}_{1}^{37} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{12}[(37)^{3/2}-1] \\  & =\frac{\pi (37\sqrt{37}-1)}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186278408 :question/id #uuid "7d00a6aa-63ec-5be5-aa3c-4e85a0b4a1af" :question/math-academy-id "q-161174" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186176065 :knowledge-point/id #uuid 0,\,z\ge 0.$" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ defined by $x=f(y,z)$ with $(y,z)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂x}{∂y})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂x}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
x=2-y-z,\,(y,z)\in D
$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D={(y,z)\,:\,{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}\le 1,\,y\ge 0,\,z\ge 0},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/37/3741c5db05232f04f60f747dc04176bfc77da30bbc39c79888cf4c18939369f7.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2-y-z)=-1, \\ \frac{∂x}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(2-y-z)=-1,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂x}{∂y})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂x}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(-1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+1+1}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{3}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region $D$ can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 1,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\sqrt{3}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\sqrt{3}\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{1}r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\,\text{d}\theta {\int }_{0}^{1}r\,\text{d}r \\  & =\sqrt{3}\cdot [\theta ]_{0}^{\pi /2}\cdot {[\frac{{r}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\sqrt{3}\cdot \frac{\pi }{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{\pi \sqrt{3}}{4}.\end{aligned}

${x}^{2}+{z}^{2}\le 2.$" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ defined by $y=f(x,z)$ with $(x,z)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂y}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂y}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
y=1-{x}^{2}+{z}^{2},\,(x,z)\in D
$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D={(x,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}\le 2},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/ab/ab855ef2b9b5363005c14ea37470ed9ecb5853380a301341d20e2cd6095a5d1f.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂y}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(1-{x}^{2}+{z}^{2})=-2x, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(1-{x}^{2}+{z}^{2})=2z,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂y}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂y}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(-2x)^{2}+(2z)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4{x}^{2}+4{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4({x}^{2}+{z}^{2})}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region $D$ can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le \sqrt{2},\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4({x}^{2}+{z}^{2})}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting $u=1+4{r}^{2},$ we get $\text{d}u=8r\,\text{d}r.$ Also, the limits must be changed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & 0 & \sqrt{2} \\ u & 1 & 9\end{aligned}
$$

 

Substituting these into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r & =2\pi \cdot \frac{1}{8}{\int }_{1}^{9}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}{\int }_{1}^{9}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}\cdot \frac{2}{3}{[{u}^{3/2}]}_{1}^{9} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}{[{u}^{3/2}]}_{1}^{9} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}(27-1) \\  & =\frac{13\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186415937 :question/id #uuid "139ae790-9731-55fc-ab5e-266ae6726353" :question/math-academy-id "q-109765"} {:db/id 17592186415939 :question/id #uuid parametrized by a differentiable vector-valued function

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v) = \big\langle x(u,v), \: y(u,v), \: z(u,v) \big\rangle
$$

defined over a region $D$ in the $uv$-plane, then the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_{S} \: \textrm{d}S =  \iint\limits_{D} \| \mathbf{r}'_ u \times \mathbf{r}'_v  \| \: \textrm{d}A,
$$

where $\mathbf{r}'_ u \times \mathbf{r}'_v$ is the fundamental vector product of the surface.

$$

The surface $S$ shown above consists of the part of the paraboloid $z=x^2+y^2$ that lies under the plane $z=9.$ Let's compute the surface area of $S.$

The plane intersects the paraboloid when $z=9.$ Thus, the curve that describes the intersection points is

$$
x^2+y^2 = 9,
$$

which is a circle of radius $3$ in the $xy$-plane. 

Therefore, our surface can be described by the equations

$$
z = f(x,y) = x^2 + y^2, \quad (x,y) \in D
$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D = \left\{(x,y): \, x^2 + y^2 \le 9\right\}.
$$

To compute the surface area of $S,$ we use the formula

$$
\iint\limits_S \,  \text{d}S = \iint\limits_D \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A.
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2x, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2y\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these expressions into our surface area formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(2x)^{2}+(2y)^{2}}\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}}\,dA.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, by changing the variables to polar coordinates $(x,y)\to (r,\theta),$ we have $\textrm dA = r\,\textrm d r\, \textrm d \theta.$ Thus, our integration region becomes

$$
\Delta = \left\{(r,\theta): \, 0\leq r\leq 3,\:0\leq\theta\lt 2\pi\right\}.
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}}\,dA & ={∬}_{Δ}\sqrt{1+4(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+4(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,r\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}\,}\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,d\theta \,{\int }_{0}^{3}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}\,}\,dr \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}\,}\,dr \\  & =2\pi {[\frac{1}{12}{(1+4{r}^{2})}^{3/2}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}{[{(1+4{r}^{2})}^{3/2}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}(37\sqrt{37}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

So, we conclude that the area of our surface is 

$$
\iint\limits_S \,  \text{d}S =  \dfrac{\pi}{6}(37\sqrt{37} -1).
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1f3795a6-1971-55b3-9109-8565cd3830a4" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5344 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"} :step/id #uuid "20aafc3a-c734-59a5-9792-c59b83342b12" :step/math-academy-id 33441 :step/next {:db/id 17592186176721}} {:db/id 17592186176747 :step/content {:db/id 17592186175996 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186175848 :question/id #uuid "77e8fb3e-1858-5831-b740-a0c133c8180f" :question/math-academy-id "e-9141"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b8c0f4b8-0b77-5e8a-aae2-2d27ea125d82" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049997}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186176212} {:db/id 17592186176243} {:db/id 17592186278397} {:db/id 17592186278398} {:db/id 17592186278400} {:db/id 17592186278413} {:db/id 17592186389160} {:db/id 17592186389167} {:db/id 17592186415936}] :knowledge-point/title "Surface Areas of Surfaces Defined as Z=F(X,Y): Non-Rectangular Domains"} :step/id #uuid "dd0b86de-1ce8-5231-a10e-a2cb302f264c" :step/math-academy-id 34075 :step/next {:db/id 17592186176887}} {:db/id 17592186176884 :step/content {:db/id 17592186176065 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186175710 :question/id #uuid "7498df7d-a340-599e-b4ba-496f5142c28c" :question/math-academy-id "e-12379"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "2966982a-a726-53e7-923f-2ca43760b756" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049084}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186176248} {:db/id 17592186176395} {:db/id 17592186278404} {:db/id 17592186278405} {:db/id 17592186278406} {:db/id 17592186278407} {:db/id 17592186278408} {:db/id 17592186278409} {:db/id 17592186415937} {:db/id 17592186415939}] :knowledge-point/title "Changing to Polar Coordinates"} :step/id #uuid "95a582e7-cf2f-5cb4-a271-ae31cf32d50a" :step/math-academy-id 44417} {:db/id 17592186176887 :step/content {:db/id 17592186177075 :tutorial/content "We have similar formulas for the areas of surfaces defined by $x = f(y,z)$ and $y = f(x,z){:}$

\iint\limits_S \,  \text{d}S = \iint\limits_D \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A.
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2x, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2y\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these expressions into our surface area formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(2x)^{2}+(2y)^{2}}\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}}\,dA.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, by changing the variables to polar coordinates $(x,y)\to (r,\theta),$ we have $\textrm dA = r\,\textrm d r\, \textrm d \theta.$ Thus, our integration region becomes

$$
\Delta = \left\{(r,\theta): \, 0\leq r\leq 3,\:0\leq\theta\lt 2\pi\right\}.
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}}\,dA & ={∬}_{Δ}\sqrt{1+4(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+4(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,r\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}\,}\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,d\theta \,{\int }_{0}^{3}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}\,}\,dr \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}\,}\,dr \\  & =2\pi {[\frac{1}{12}{(1+4{r}^{2})}^{3/2}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}{[{(1+4{r}^{2})}^{3/2}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}(37\sqrt{37}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

So, we conclude that the area of our surface is 

$$
\iint\limits_S \,  \text{d}S =  \dfrac{\pi}{6}(37\sqrt{37} -1).
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1f3795a6-1971-55b3-9109-8565cd3830a4" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5344 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"} {:db/id 17592186176887 :step/content {:db/id 17592186177075 :tutorial/content "We have similar formulas for the areas of surfaces defined by $x = f(y,z)$ and $y = f(x,z){:}$
